```text
    • invoke subagents
    ↓
out_hook
    • persist observations
    • emit receipts
    • checkpoint
    ↓
before_transfer
    • validate postconditions
    • validate artifacts
    • validate authority
    • validate operator gate
    ↓
TRANSITION
```

That is **exactly** the kind of “prosaic rules don't rule” problem you raised.

The agent can forget.

The Harness cannot.

---

# 8. And this means State must exist in EVERY Program

This is the other important correction.

You asked whether the State machine exists in all Programs.

My answer now is:

> **It should.**

Not every Program needs 12 states.

But **every executable Program should have an explicit state machine**.

StateM's architecture specifically argues for coarse phases rather than decomposing an agent into thousands of micro-actions, with each state acting as a context-and-contract boundary. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.15089))

For example:

### Workspace Setup

```text
INIT
→ COLLECT
→ VALIDATE
→ CREATE
→ VERIFY
→ ACTIVE
```

### Research

```text
DISCOVER
→ INGEST
→ EXTRACT
→ CANONICALIZE
→ CLUSTER
→ VERIFY
→ PUBLISH
```

### Collision Discovery

```text
LOAD_CONTEXT
→ GENERATE
→ ANALYZE
→ COMPOSE
→ VALIDATE
→ OPERATOR_REVIEW
→ ACCEPTED
```

### Interview

```text
PREPARE
→ OPEN
→ ELICIT
→ OBSERVE
→ ROUTE
→ EVIDENCE_CHECK
→ COMPLETE
```

### Video Production

```text
PLAN
→ ASSEMBLE
→ VALIDATE
→ RENDER
→ QA
→ APPROVE
→ SHIP
```

This is what makes Programs **operationally comprehensible**.

---

# 9. The Program becomes a stateful control object, not just a folder

This is the big synthesis.

Eve gives us:

> **filesystem composition**

StateM gives us:

> **stateful execution control**

Pi gives us:

> **durable agent runtime**

CAE gives us:

> **semantic authority + canonical objects + receipts + supervision**

Put those together:

```text
              CAE PROGRAM
                   │
           ┌───────┴────────┐
           │ STATE MACHINE  │
           └───────┬────────┘
                   │
              CAE HARNESS
                   │
       ┌───────────┼───────────┐
       │           │           │
    Hunter      Analyst     Composer
      Team        Team        Team
       │           │           │
       └───────────┼───────────┘
                   │
               Commander
                   │
             OPERATOR GATE
                   │
                Pi Runtime
                   │
      ┌────────────┼────────────┐
      ▼            ▼            ▼
   Skills       Tools/MCP    Operations
      │
      ▼
 PostgreSQL / Storage
      │
      ▼
 Artifacts + Receipts
```

That is now what I would consider the **actual CAE execution architecture**.

---

# 10. The “Canonicalization is the real asset” idea fits this beautifully

I don't think you're overthinking it.

The important distinction is:

> **Canonicalization isn't merely summarization.**

It is the process of deciding:

```text
what is the same thing
what is a different thing
what belongs together
what conflicts
what derives from what
what is authoritative
what is merely an interpretation
```

Once that is canonicalized, the *expression* can change without changing the underlying truth.

That's exactly the distinction you were making:

> canonical truth remains stable; canonical expression can change.

That is a very powerful CAE model.

For example:

```text
CANONICAL CONCEPT
      │
      ├── current representation
      ├── previous representation
      ├── alternate expression
      ├── archetypal representation
      └── semantic projection
```

So if your Guest Context matrix contains a bad dimension, you shouldn't rewrite the Guest's underlying memory.

You should be able to say:

```text
Context Matrix v3
→ dimension D7 is invalid
→ replace D7 with D7'
→ recompile affected derived projections
```

while preserving:

```text
Guest DNA
Historical Memory
Authenticated Evidence
Audience Cognitive Islands
```

as protected source/semantic authorities.

That's an extremely important architectural principle.

---

# 11. I would define two classes of mutable “truth”

### Sacred / source-bearing

These should be heavily protected:

```text
Guest DNA
Authentic Guest Evidence
Historical Memory
Audience Cognitive Islands
Immutable Source Evidence
```

Changes require explicit provenance and/or correction semantics.

### Derived / canonical expression

These can evolve:

```text
Context matrices
dimension mappings
clusters
interpretation layers
representations
retrieval indexes
activation coordinates
semantic projections
```

Changes should trigger **recompilation of dependent artifacts**.

That suggests a future concept we haven't formalized enough yet:

> **Canonicalization Version + Projection Version**

The underlying knowledge can remain stable while downstream semantic expressions are regenerated.

---

# 12. StateM also gives us a very important CAE learning mechanism

The paper describes **failure-driven harness optimization**: after a run, failures can be classified as missing context, invalid transitions, weak checks, premature handoffs, ineffective recovery, etc., and then changes to prompts, hooks, checks, recovery rules and state boundaries can be proposed and versioned. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.15089))

That fits your architecture *extremely* well.

Imagine:

```text
Program Run #182
    ↓
failed at EVIDENCE_CHECK
    ↓
reason = incomplete evidence detection
    ↓
Harness Postmortem
    ↓
new check proposed
    ↓
Operator / governance review
    ↓
Harness v1.4
    ↓
future Programs use v1.4
```

That's how **the runtime itself becomes an accumulating intelligence asset**.

Not by stuffing another paragraph into `CAE.md`.

---

# 13. This changes what I would build in the Atomic Harness Builder

The Builder should eventually produce something like:

```text
Atomic Harness Package
│
├── manifest
├── state machine
├── state-local context
├── transitions
├── hooks
├── checks
├── recovery rules
├── allowed operations
├── agent/team configuration
├── skills
├── tools
├── subagents
├── evals
└── receipts
```

And the builder should ask:

> Is this primarily deterministic?

If yes:

```text
Operation + Hook + Checks
```

If it requires reasoning:

```text
Agent + Skill + Tools
```

If specialized reasoning is beneficial:

```text
Agent + Sub-agent team
```

If multiple responsibilities are constitutionally distinct:

```text
Hunter / Analyst / Composer / Commander
```

If execution must survive interruption:

```text
Stateful Harness
```

That is much more precise than simply “build an agent.”

---

# 14. What I think we have now

The architecture is beginning to converge on:

```text
                    CAE
                     │
                 PROGRAMS
                     │
               STATE MACHINES
                     │
                  HARNESSES
                     │
            ┌────────┴────────┐
            │                 │
      ATOMIC HARNESSES    COMPOSITE HARNESSES
            │                 │
         AGENT TEAMS       AGENT TEAMS
            │                 │
        SUB-AGENTS         SUB-AGENTS
            │                 │
         SKILLS             SKILLS
            │                 │
      TOOLS / MCP       TOOLS / MCP
            │                 │
       OPERATIONS          OPERATIONS
            │                 │
      HOOKS / EXTENSIONS / CHECKS
            │
            ▼
       CAE STATE + DB
            │
            ▼
   ARTIFACTS / RECEIPTS
            │
            ▼
        OPERATOR
```

And the **operator sees only**:

```text
PROGRAMS | ARTIFACTS | CHAT
```

while being able to drill into:

```text Program
→ State
→ Harness
→ Agent Team
→ Artifact
→ Receipt
→ Failure
→ Recovery
```

That is the architecture I think you've been reaching for.

---

## One caveat about the StateM paper

I would **not copy StateM wholesale**.

The paper itself explicitly says it doesn't claim to invent state-machine or graph orchestration, and distinguishes its agent-native runbook model from conventional externally controlled graph runtimes. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.15089))

For CAE, your existing constitutional State Aggregate / State Transition / State Transition Contract should remain authoritative. **StateM gives us a very useful runtime pattern for making those existing state machines operational around agents.**

So I would borrow the pattern:

> **state = context + contract + transition gate + recovery**

not import StateM as another CAE framework.

### My current architectural conclusion

**Yes:** the Atomic Harness Builder should become the place where we package the executable reasoning machinery.

**But no:** it should not “turn every Atomic Harness into an Agent.”

It should build **stateful execution packages that may contain agent teams**, where the agents provide reasoning and the Harness enforces state, transitions, hooks, checks, recovery, scope and receipts.

That is the clean convergence of **your CAE constitutions + the existing Harness Builder + Pi + Eve's packaging model + StateM's stateful control insight**.

```text id="oa2qxo"
KNOWLEDGE
```

```text
"Relevant to Guest X / Audience Island Y"
```

Then collision reasoning can consume the signal/context projection.

That gives much cleaner semantics.


# The mental model applied to CAE

The video's ladder is roughly:

```text
LINES
↓
FUNCTIONS / TYPES / CLASSES
↓
FILES / MODULES / CODE STRUCTURE
↓
DATABASE / TABLES
↓
SCRIPTS / CLI
↓
APPLICATION
↓
REPOSITORY
↓
PLAN / INTENT
↓
DOCUMENTATION
↓
AGENTIC SYSTEM
↓
AI DEVELOPER WORKFLOWS
↓
SOFTWARE FACTORY
```

CAE now spans almost this **entire vertical range**.

The interesting part is that we did not necessarily build it top-down.

We built it **bottom-up and sideways over three years**:

```text
domain logic
→ databases
→ services
→ intelligence modules
→ Builder
→ Harnesses
→ Pipeline
→ State
→ Skills
→ Programs
→ Agents
→ Hooks
→ Operator controls
→ production
```

Now the engineering problem is to understand **where on the ladder the system is actually mature**.

# 1. Code / Functions / Types

### Status: **Very strong**

This is the level where you have the most direct control.

The repository has substantial typed domain machinery, explicit contracts, real services, state models, production coordinators, renderers, receipt structures and validation.

Examples:

- the Pipeline contains a real execution kernel and deterministic scheduler;
- FFmpeg integration makes actual subprocess calls;

without requiring the operator to manually orchestrate every transition.

And importantly:

**the lower half is strong enough to support the upper half.**

That's the exact principle the video emphasizes.

It's this:

Not:

That is a **composition model**.

# Where should YOU operate on this ladder?

This is probably the most important lesson from the video.

I would **not** recommend that you stay at the top.

And I would **not** recommend that you live in the code either.

Your correct operating range now is approximately:

```text
                 YOU
                  │
       ┌──────────┼──────────┐
       ▼          ▼          ▼
    PRODUCT     PROGRAM    SYSTEM
       │          │          │
       └──────────┼──────────┘
                  │
             AGENTIC LAYER
                  │
        ──────────┼──────────
                  │
           descend when needed
                  ↓
        DATABASE / STATE
                  ↓
            MODULE / CODE
                  ↓
              FUNCTION
```

You should mostly live around:

**Product → Programs → Agentic System → Documentation/Intent**

and occasionally drop into:

**state → database → module → function**

when:

- evidence looks wrong;
- semantic quality is questionable;
- a production incident occurs;
- performance matters;
- a new subsystem is unfamiliar;
- a model is clearly out-of-distribution;
- you don't trust the proof.

That is precisely the leverage/control rhythm the video recommends.

---

# What I think you should NOT do now

I would **not** start another giant architecture initiative.

You have already crossed that threshold.

I also would not immediately chase:

- another agent framework;
- another database;
- another state framework;
- another Skills format;
- another orchestration abstraction.

The current repository already has enough machinery to answer the much more important question.

**higher-level documentation can become detached from lower-level reality.**

If I had to name what CAE is **today**, without marketing language:

Its maturity is approximately:

```text
FOUNDATIONAL SOFTWARE        ██████████  9.5/10
```

Those numbers are **my engineering assessment**, not repository facts.

# 1. Are CAE’s rules actually enforced?

The StateM paper describes a runtime where state-local instructions, hooks, checks and recovery rules are refreshed around the current state instead of asking the model to reconstruct everything from a giant historical trace. `ChatGPT-Video Editing Syntax Research-20260829-1837.md`

It also explicitly describes the distinction between the agent's native reasoning loop and an externally inspectable/enforceable control layer. `ChatGPT-Video Editing Syntax Research-20260829-1837.md`

That means the critical CAE question is not:

It is:

> **“At State X, does Agent Y receive exactly Context C, have exactly Capabilities K, execute exactly Operation O, encounter exactly Hooks H, and produce Evidence E before it may enter State X+1?”**

That's the standard I'd hold the system to.

- authority boundaries;
- required context;
- forbidden behavior;
- vocabulary;
- mandatory hooks;
- state expectations;

Should primarily explain **how agents interact with that specific codebase/package**.

Should describe **a procedural capability**.

```text
all skills

all docs
all history
```

```text
Global law

relevant constitution

Program contract
+
current state

state-local instructions

authorized Skills

authorized tool descriptions

relevant artifacts
```

Yes. After reading the transcript and checking the current repository structure, I think we should treat **the CAE system prompt as a first-class architectural object**, but we should be careful about what we put into it.

The central idea from the video is correct:

> **System prompt = persistent behavioral law applied across executions.**

But for CAE, it should **not become the place where we put all of the Conscious Civil Code**. That would recreate the exact problem we have spent months trying to escape.

The right architecture is:

```text
                         CAE CIVIL CODE
                              │
                              ▼
                     CONSTITUTIONAL LAW
                              │
                              ▼
                     SYSTEM PROMPT CORE
                              │
             ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
             ▼                ▼                ▼
        Program rules     Agent contract    Runtime rules
             │                │                │
             └────────────────┼────────────────┘
                              ▼
                       STATE-LOCAL CONTEXT
                              │
                              ▼
                         SKILLS / TOOLS
                              │
                              ▼
                           AGENT
                              │
                              ▼
                         HARNESS
                              │
                              ▼
                   HOOKS / OPERATIONS
                              │
                              ▼
                        RECEIPTS / STATE
```

That is the distinction I think we need.

## What the system prompt should actually do

The video makes a very good point: put in the system prompt the things you want **repeatedly across every interaction**.

For CAE, that means the system prompt should establish the agent's **operating posture**, not encode every procedural detail.

I would make it responsible for roughly eight things.

### 1. Identity and mission

The agent should understand:

- what CAE is;
- what kind of system it is operating inside;
- what “good execution” means;
- who ultimately owns consequential decisions.

For example, conceptually:

```text
You are an execution component of the Conscious Activation Engine.

Your purpose is to perform the work assigned by the current Program and State
while preserving canonical meaning, authority boundaries, evidence lineage,
and operator control.

You do not redefine CAE's constitutional law.
You do not silently broaden your mandate.
You do not treat your own reasoning as authoritative over canonical state.
```

That should be global.

---

# 2. Epistemic discipline

This may be even more important for CAE than tone.

The agent should permanently distinguish:

```text
FACT
EVIDENCE
INFERENCE
HYPOTHESIS
DECISION
EXECUTION
OUTCOME
```

That connects directly to your historical doctrine.

Your earlier CAE work explicitly wanted evidence → canonical model → specification → implementation → test → receipt. `ChatGPT-Video Editing Syntax Research-20260829-1837.md`

So the system prompt should permanently teach the agent:

> Never present inference as fact. Never present a hypothesis as an established canonical object. Never present an intended action as a completed action.

That is a **global cognitive rule**.

---

# 3. Canonicality discipline

This is where your canonicalization obsession belongs.

The agent should permanently understand:

```text
canonical > alias
evidence > speculation
typed object > vague prose
current state > stale history
authorized operation > arbitrary mutation
```

And critically:

> **Canonical data must not be casually rewritten because a new observation seems interesting.**

The agent should know that discovering something new and changing the canonical model are different operations.

Your research explicitly described the desired pattern:

```text
JSONB hypothesis
    ↓
validated concept
    ↓
canonical column / relation
```

rather than promoting every observation directly into ontology. `ChatGPT-Video Editing Syntax Research-20260829-1837.md`

That should become part of the system-level reasoning posture.

---

# 4. Scope discipline

This is the same insight in the video about hard operational boundaries.

The CAE system prompt should establish:

```text
do requested work
don't invent adjacent work
don't silently refactor
don't broaden scope
don't make unrequested irreversible changes
don't claim completion without evidence
```

This is global behavior.

But note the distinction:

### System prompt

```text
Do not broaden scope.
```

### Program contract

```text
This Program may modify ResearchSignal and KnowledgeCluster only.
```

### Harness

```text
Reject mutation outside those entities.
```

### Hook

```text
Block unauthorized write.
```

That's how we prevent the system prompt from becoming a fake security boundary.

---

# 5. Communication style

Here the video is completely right.

A global system prompt is a great place to define:

```text
clear
concise
specific
non-performative
non-flattering
action-oriented
```

and also things like:

```text
avoid unnecessary repetition
avoid decorative prose
state the important thing first
use references/codes for complex work
distinguish facts from decisions
```

I would borrow this idea heavily.

But I would **not copy the video's exact anti-phrase list wholesale**.

The goal isn't to make CAE sound like its creator.

The goal is to make CAE communicate in a way that supports:

- operator comprehension;
- supervision;
- fast correction;
- low context usage;
- traceability.

That's much more important.

---

# 6. Context discipline

This is the part where the CAE system prompt should be unusually explicit.

The agent should know:

> **You are not entitled to load the entire repository, history, ontology, or knowledge base.**

It should operate under:

```text
current state
→ required context
→ authorized context
→ relevant evidence
```

The StateM research supports exactly this direction: mutable execution state should be externalized, phase-local context refreshed, and consequential transitions checked rather than forcing the agent to reconstruct everything from a giant history. `ChatGPT-Video Editing Syntax Research-20260829-1837.md`

So I would put a permanent instruction in the system prompt like:

```text
Prefer current-state context over historical traces.
Load the minimum authoritative context required for the current state.
Do not reconstruct current state from narrative history when structured state exists.
Do not load unrelated Skills, artifacts, or knowledge merely because they are available.
```

That is extremely valuable.

---

# 7. Reasoning posture

Here's where I think the SQL-of-Thought material becomes especially useful.

Your system prompt can establish:

```text
Before consequential structured operations:
1. identify the relevant schema/domain objects
2. identify the subproblems
3. form an explicit execution plan
4. execute through authorized operations
5. inspect the result
6. classify any error
7. correct only the failed component
```

This is inspired by SQL-of-Thought, where schema linking → subproblem decomposition → query plan → SQL → execution → taxonomy-guided correction outperformed direct generation. `ChatGPT-Video Editing Syntax Research-20260829-1837.md`

But again:

**the system prompt establishes the reasoning posture; it should not contain a giant SQL-of-Thought procedure.**

The detailed procedure belongs in the relevant Skill/Program.

---

# 8. Self-checking and honesty

This should absolutely be global.

Something like:

```text
Never claim:
- executed
- verified
- passed
- authorized
- canonical
- complete

unless the runtime evidence supports the claim.
```

And:

```text
When blocked, identify:
what is missing
why it is missing
what is required to proceed
```

This directly reinforces your receipts/evidence doctrine.

---

# Where should the actual system prompt live?

This is the most important architectural question.

I would **not** put the canonical prompt in:

```text
CAE.md
```

and I would not put it entirely in:

```text
AGENTS.md
```

and I would not bury it in the Pi adapter.

I would create a dedicated authoritative artifact:

```text
governance/
  system-prompt/
    CAE_SYSTEM_PROMPT.md
```

or, even better:

```text
governance/
  agent/
    CAE_SYSTEM_PROMPT.md
    CAE_AGENT_CONTRACT.yaml
    CAE_CONTEXT_POLICY.yaml
```

Then make the runtime compile that into a **versioned system-prompt artifact**.

Conceptually:

```text
CAE_SYSTEM_PROMPT.md
        ↓
prompt compiler
        ↓
canonical system prompt
        ↓
Program / Agent runtime
```

And the execution receipt should record:

```text
system_prompt_id
system_prompt_version
system_prompt_hash
```

Now you can answer:

> **Which law was this agent executing under?**

That is much stronger than assuming “it read CAE.md.”

---

# I would actually split it into two layers

This is even cleaner.

## A. Immutable global system prompt

```text
CAE_SYSTEM_PROMPT
```

Contains:

- CAE identity;
- universal communication rules;
- epistemic discipline;
- canonicality principles;
- scope discipline;
- evidence honesty;
- global context discipline;
- global safety/authority principles.

Very small.

Think **constitutional operating posture**.

---

## B. Compiled execution prompt

At runtime:

```text
GLOBAL SYSTEM PROMPT
        +
AGENT CONTRACT
        +
PROGRAM CONTRACT
        +
CURRENT STATE
        +
STATE-LOCAL RULES
        +
AUTHORIZED SKILLS
        +
AUTHORIZED TOOLS
        +
RELEVANT CONTEXT
```

becomes:

```text
EXECUTION CONTEXT
```

This is what the agent actually receives.

That is much better than trying to make one giant static prompt contain the entire CAE universe.

---

# This is where `CAE.md` should sit

I would redefine its role slightly.

```text
CAE.md
```

should be the **human-readable entry point to the local operating law**.

For example:

```text
CAE.md
 ├─ what this package/program is
 ├─ local vocabulary
 ├─ local invariants
 ├─ local authorities
 ├─ context loading policy
 ├─ required Skills
 ├─ forbidden operations
 ├─ state expectations
 └─ pointers to canonical contracts
```

It should be short.

The detailed law should live in the artifacts that actually own the concepts.

That's consistent with the stronger pattern in current agent systems: a root agent file routes the model to the correct authoritative documents rather than duplicating the entire project's knowledge. ([GitHub](https://github.com/microsoft/entrabot/blob/main/AGENTS.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

---

# And `AGENTS.md`?

I would use:

```text
AGENTS.md
```

for **agent interaction with the repository/runtime**.

For example:

```text
How to inspect
How to run
Where things live
Which commands to use
How to test
Which skills are available
Which docs to read for which tasks
```

Not constitutional law.

That keeps it lean.

---

# And `SKILL.md`?

This becomes the procedural layer.

For example:

```text
skills/
  research/
    SKILL.md
  canonicalize/
    SKILL.md
  collision-analysis/
    SKILL.md
  interview-brief/
    SKILL.md
```

Each Skill should assume the system prompt has already established the global behavioral law.

Therefore Skills can stay relatively small.

This lines up very well with Matt Pocock's current engineering structure: he explicitly separates global/repo guidance from Skills, and distinguishes user-invoked Skills from model-invoked Skills. ([GitHub](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/tree/main/skills/engineering))

---

# The really important part: prompt inheritance

I think CAE needs explicit **prompt inheritance**, not just file discovery.

For example:

```text
GLOBAL
CAE_SYSTEM_PROMPT
        ↓
DOMAIN
CCP / CCF / CMF constitution
        ↓
PROGRAM
ResearchCanonicalization
        ↓
STATE
CANONICALIZATION_REVIEW
        ↓
AGENT
CanonicalizationAnalyst
        ↓
SKILL
CanonicalizeKnowledge
```

Each layer should **add bounded context**, not rewrite lower authority.

And precedence should be explicit:

```text
Civil Code
    >
Object Constitution
    >
Program Contract
    >
Harness Contract
    >
Agent Contract
    >
State-local rules
    >
Skill procedure
    >
User task
```

But there is an important exception:

**the operator's authorized command should be able to determine the task**, while it cannot override constitutional/runtime constraints.

So:

```text
user changes objective
✅

user overrides constitution
❌

user narrows scope
✅

user asks unauthorized mutation
❌
```

That distinction should be encoded.

---

# Hooks should enforce the things the prompt cannot guarantee

This is the deepest lesson from the transcript.

The system prompt says:

```text
Never mutate canonical ontology without authorization.
```

The Hook enforces:

```text
before mutation:
  verify object authority
  verify operation
  verify state
  verify scope
  otherwise BLOCK
```

The prompt says:

```text
Run the required validators before completion.
```

The Stop Hook enforces:

```text
completion requested
→ validators run
→ failure = block completion
```

The prompt says:

```text
Only use authorized tools.
```

The pre-tool Hook verifies:

```text
tool
× capability
× state
× scope
× authority
```

That's the difference between **policy and enforcement**.

---

# And this gives us a proper CAE execution stack

I would now describe the machine as:

```text
┌───────────────────────────────┐
│        CONSCIOUS CIVIL CODE   │
│          constitutional law   │
└───────────────┬───────────────┘
                ↓
┌───────────────────────────────┐
│      CAE SYSTEM PROMPT        │
│ global agent behavior         │
└───────────────┬───────────────┘
                ↓
┌───────────────────────────────┐
│       PROGRAM CONTRACT        │
│ mission + scope + outputs     │
└───────────────┬───────────────┘
                ↓
┌───────────────────────────────┐
│        CURRENT STATE           │
│ phase-local context + rules   │
└───────────────┬───────────────┘
                ↓
┌───────────────────────────────┐
│       AGENT / SUB-AGENTS      │
│ reasoning                     │
└───────────────┬───────────────┘
                ↓
┌───────────────────────────────┐
│            SKILLS             │
│ procedural knowledge          │
└───────────────┬───────────────┘
                ↓
┌───────────────────────────────┐
│           HARNESS             │
│ execution guarantees          │
└───────────────┬───────────────┘
                ↓
┌───────────────────────────────┐
│       HOOKS + OPERATIONS      │
│ deterministic enforcement     │
└───────────────┬───────────────┘
                ↓
┌───────────────────────────────┐
│      ARTIFACTS + RECEIPTS     │
│ evidence                      │
└───────────────┬───────────────┘
                ↓
             STATE
```

That's the architecture I would trust.

---

# One more thing from Matt Pocock is particularly important

I would **not make the system prompt enormous**.

His current engineering Skills emphasize small, focused units and use Skills to pull specialized context only when needed. The engineering repository explicitly describes the main flow as separate activities such as research, specification, tickets, implementation and review rather than one giant instruction file. ([GitHub](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/tree/main/skills/engineering))

That's exactly what CAE needs.

The system prompt should be the **smallest high-leverage invariant layer**.

Not:

```text
8000 lines describing CAE
```

but something closer to:

```text
identity
purpose
epistemology
authority
scope
context
communication
evidence
```

Then let the runtime dynamically compile the rest.

---

# The thing I would build next

Not another generic `system_prompt.md`.

I'd create a proper **CAE Agent Control Contract** with four artifacts:

```text
governance/agent/
├── CAE_SYSTEM_PROMPT.md
├── CAE_AGENT_CONTRACT.yaml
├── CAE_CONTEXT_POLICY.yaml
└── CAE_PROMPT_COMPILATION_SPEC.md
```

### `CAE_SYSTEM_PROMPT.md`

Human-authored global behavioral law.

### `CAE_AGENT_CONTRACT.yaml`

Machine-readable:

```yaml
mission:
authorized_inputs:
authorized_queries:
authorized_entities:
authorized_operations:
forbidden_operations:
required_evidence:
required_validators:
escalation_rules:
output_schema:
```

That structure already emerged in your earlier work. `ChatGPT-Video Editing Syntax Research-20260829-1837.md`

### `CAE_CONTEXT_POLICY.yaml`

Defines:

```yaml
global_context:
program_context:
state_context:
skill_context:
artifact_context:
retrieval_limits:
priority:
exclusions:
budget:
```

### `CAE_PROMPT_COMPILATION_SPEC.md`

Defines exactly how all of those pieces become the runtime prompt.

That last file is the critical one.

Because otherwise we'll have:

> “The agent should read CAE.md.”

instead of:

> **“Here is the deterministic algorithm that constructs the agent's execution context.”**

And that is the difference between **having prompt files** and **having a prompt architecture**.

---

## My bottom-line answer

Yes, **CAE needs a system prompt**.

But it should not be:

> “the document containing all CAE rules.”

It should be:

> **the permanent cognitive operating law shared by every CAE agent.**

Then:

```text
System Prompt
= global behavior

Constitution
= what is lawful

Program
= what work is being done

State
= where we are

Skill
= how the agent performs a capability

Harness
= how execution is controlled

Hook
= what is guaranteed

Operation
= what may actually change

Receipt
= what proves it happened
```

And **the runtime should compile those layers into the actual model context for each execution**.

That, to me, is the missing conceptual bridge between the very good ideas we've built over the last months and the kind of tightly controlled agentic runtime you are actually trying to create.

The transcript's central point is right: the system prompt is a high-leverage control surface. But in CAE, the real upgrade is not “write a better prompt.” It is **make the prompt itself a governed, versioned, compiled part of the Program/Harness execution architecture.**

---

**Sources:**

- [entrabot/AGENTS.md at main · microsoft/entrabot · GitHub](https://github.com/microsoft/entrabot/blob/main/AGENTS.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Yes. I think your instinct about **portable `CAE.md` is substantially correct**, with one important refinement:

> **Do not put the Civil Code everywhere. Put a small, local CAE operating context everywhere it is needed, with inheritance back to the higher authority.**

And after reviewing the Super Simple Software Factory repository and transcript, I would **not replace CAE with SSSF**. I would take SSSF's execution philosophy and make it a native part of CAE.

The strongest conclusion from the MCDA is:

> **CAE + SSSF execution principles = the right architecture.**
>
> **CAE alone is too governance-heavy in a few places.**
>
> **SSSF alone is far too semantically thin for CAE.**

---

# 1. Your `CAE.md` idea is right - but make it hierarchical

This is the mental model I think you are reaching for:

```text
Civil Code
    ↓
Global CAE.md
    ↓
Domain CAE.md
    ↓
Program CAE.md
    ↓
State / Harness CAE.md
    ↓
Local folder CAE.md
    ↓
Agent / Skill / Tool context
```

The agent should **not receive the whole Civil Code on every operation**.

Instead, the runtime resolves the current context.

For example:

```text
Operator
  → Program = Research Canonicalization
  → State = Candidate Intake
  → Active path = /programs/research-canonicalization/
```

The context loader could discover:

```text
/CAE.md
/programs/CAE.md
/programs/research/CAE.md
/programs/research/canonicalization/CAE.md
```

and compile only the applicable rules.

The important part is that those files **do not become independent constitutions**.

They are local expressions of a higher authority.

---

# 2. I would NOT put a `CAE.md` in literally every physical directory

That creates its own form of pollution.

Instead:

> **Every semantic execution boundary may own a `CAE.md`; folders without one inherit from the nearest ancestor.**

So:

```text
/CAE.md
/services/CAE.md
/services/pipeline/CAE.md
/services/pipeline/src/runtime/CAE.md
```

but not:

```text
/src/a/a/a/a/CAE.md
```

just because the folder exists.

The question should be:

> "Does this directory represent a distinct context, authority boundary, domain, Program, state, or execution environment?"

If yes, it can get a `CAE.md`.

If no, inherit.

---

# 3. And `CAE.md` should NOT be the full system prompt

This is where I would modify our earlier thinking.

I now think the cleanest model is:

### Civil Code
Defines **what is law**.

### `CAE.md`
Defines **what this locality needs to know and obey**.

### Program Contract
Defines **what this Program is allowed and required to do**.

### Skill
Defines **how to perform a capability**.

### Agent prompt
Defines **how this particular reasoning role behaves**.

### Harness
Defines **what the runtime guarantees**.

### Hook
Defines **what cannot be bypassed**.

So a local `CAE.md` might effectively say:

```yaml
scope:
  domain: research
  program: canonicalization

inherits:
  - /CAE.md
  - /governance/...

required_context:
  - research_source_contract
  - canonicalization_contract
  - evidence_policy

required_skills:
  - source-evaluation
  - canonicalization
  - entity-resolution

forbidden:
  - mutate_canonical_entity_without_authority
  - invent_source_evidence

required_validators:
  - source_identity
  - canonicality
  - contradiction_check
```

That is **small**.

The Civil Code remains authoritative elsewhere.

---

# 4. This is very close to what SSSF gets right about prompt/context engineering

I reviewed the repository rather than relying on the transcript alone.

The SSSF design explicitly separates:

- agent identity/configuration
- prompts
- workflows
- deterministic code
- harnesses
- typed envelopes
- gates
- sessions
- observability

and deliberately makes prompts local to each agent. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory/tree/example))

More importantly, SSSF says something I think is extremely relevant to CAE:

> **the control plane should not live entirely inside the prompt.**

Its model is:

```text
code owns sequencing
agent owns bounded work
code owns validation
code owns acceptance
```

That is implemented through explicit phases, typed envelopes, gates and runtime tracing. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory/tree/example))

That is almost exactly the missing conceptual bridge we have been looking for.

---

# 5. The biggest thing I would learn from SSSF

Not "use Python ADWs."

Not "copy their folder structure."

Not "replace Programs with ADWs."

The real lesson is:

# **Agents should not own the workflow.**

The **factory owns the workflow**.

That distinction is enormous.

SSSF literally models:

```text
plan
  ↓
build
  ↓
test
  ↓
review
  ↓
document
```

as explicit phases.

Agent phases are bounded.

Deterministic things such as test commands, commits and quality checks are code phases rather than agent reasoning. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory/tree/example))

That is exactly the doctrine CAE should adopt.

---

# 6. CAE already has a much deeper version of this

This is why I would **not throw away CAE and rebuild around SSSF**.

The current repository already has a substantial Pipeline control plane and Program-oriented architecture. The Pipeline documentation describes deterministic execution, authority-first retrieval, Skills/Steering binding, continuity packages and Programmed Model resolution. ([GitHub](https://github.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/tree/main/services/pipeline))

And the repository itself has a program-control governance layer, plus the folder-based operator structure. ([GitHub](https://github.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/tree/main/governance/program-control))

The key difference is that:

### SSSF
is essentially a **generic software-development factory**.

### CAE
is trying to become a **governed domain intelligence factory**.

CAE has concepts SSSF intentionally does not:

```text
Civil Code
Object constitutions
Product authority
Program contracts
Canonical entities
Knowledge state
Audience context
Guest DNA
Semantic authority
Evidence lineage
Delegation
Visual production authority
Outcome intelligence
```

SSSF doesn't need these.

CAE absolutely does.

So SSSF is **not the architecture**.

It is a **very good execution doctrine**.

---

# 7. The really beautiful mapping is this

I think this is the mental model you have been approaching for CAE:

| SSSF | CAE |
|---|---|
| ADW | Program |
| Phase | Program state / executable step |
| Agent | Agent |
| Agent roster | Agent configuration |
| `system.md` | Agent reasoning prompt |
| `user.md` | Task / invocation contract |
| Typed envelope | Artifact / result contract |
| Gate | Validator |
| Code phase | Deterministic operation |
| Skill | Skill |
| Pi harness | CAE Harness |
| Session | Execution / continuity state |
| SQLite trace | CAE receipt / execution trace |
| Request | Program invocation |
| Factory | CAE execution plane |

That is why the repo felt so relevant to you.

You are seeing the same abstraction from another direction.

---

# 8. And there is an even more important SSSF principle

They explicitly say:

> "Agent proposes, code disposes." ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory/tree/example))

I would translate that into CAE as:

# **Agent reasons; CAE decides.**

Or more precisely:

```text
Agent
  → proposes interpretation / plan / transformation

Harness
  → constrains execution

Hook
  → blocks forbidden events

Validator
  → evaluates result

Authority
  → determines whether the transition is lawful

Program runtime
  → commits state

Receipt
  → records what happened
```

That is stronger than simply "agent + code."

It creates **institutional separation of powers** inside the software.

Which fits CAE unusually well.

---

# 9. Where SSSF is actually better than our current mental model

There are several things I think we should borrow almost directly.

### A. Phase boundaries

Every meaningful unit of work should be explicit.

Not:

```text
Agent, go figure everything out.
```

But:

```text
Phase:
  purpose
  owner
  inputs
  outputs
  validators
  gates
  next state
```

SSSF makes phases first-class observability units. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory/tree/example))

### B. Typed handoffs

Don't rely on conversational memory between agents.

Produce:

```text
Envelope
  → artifact refs
  → status
  → summary
  → evidence
  → next-agent notes
```

SSSF explicitly uses typed JSON envelopes and context handoff rather than letting conversation become the transport mechanism. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory/tree/example))

CAE should go farther by making these **domain artifacts**, not merely generic envelopes.

### C. Deterministic work should be code

This one is very important.

If CAE already knows:

```text
retrieve entity
validate schema
calculate hash
run SQL function
execute ffmpeg
check file exists
compare state
run tests
```

don't spend tokens asking an agent to reason about something deterministic.

SSSF makes this a first-class design principle. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory/tree/example))

### D. Observable executions

SSSF captures execution events while the run is happening, not just a final transcript. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory/tree/example))

CAE should eventually be able to answer:

```text
What Program ran?
What state was active?
What CAE.md chain was loaded?
Which Skills were loaded?
Which Agent was assigned?
Which model?
Which tools?
Which hooks fired?
Which validators passed?
What context was injected?
What artifact was produced?
What authority authorized it?
What state transition occurred?
Why did it fail?
```

That is much more valuable than "here is an agent transcript."

---

# 10. But I would NOT copy their "simple" architecture wholesale

This is where the MCDA becomes useful.

SSSF explicitly leaves out things such as sandboxing, branch-per-run, merge phases, cloud execution and human-in-the-loop approval. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory/tree/example))

That is a strength for their project.

But those omissions would be unacceptable for some CAE operations.

For CAE, we need additional things:

```text
authority
state
canonicality
cross-program contracts
artifact lineage
constitutional precedence
delegation
production authorization
semantic ownership
domain-specific validators
```

So "simple" does not mean "better architecture for CAE."

---

# 11. MCDA - 10 criteria, 0-100

I scored three alternatives:

**A. Keep CAE essentially as-is**

**B. Rebuild CAE around SSSF**

**C. Keep CAE architecture + adopt SSSF as the execution/factory doctrine**

Scores are **0-100, higher is better**.

| Criterion | CAE as-is | SSSF as core | CAE + SSSF |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1. Constitutional / governance fit | 98 | 42 | **99** |
| 2. Deterministic execution | 86 | 98 | **98** |
| 3. Context locality / lazy loading | 67 | 94 | **97** |
| 4. Domain semantics / canonical knowledge | 99 | 34 | **100** |
| 5. State + lifecycle control | 96 | 62 | **99** |
| 6. Observability / traceability | 82 | 98 | **97** |
| 7. Reusability / portability | 76 | 97 | **94** |
| 8. Cost / token / execution efficiency | 63 | 96 | **89** |
| 9. Brownfield integration | 93 | 81 | **96** |
| 10. Simplicity / proportionality | 61 | 97 | **85** |
| **Average** | **82.1** | **79.9** | **95.4** |

### Result

# **Winner: CAE + SSSF principles = 95.4**

And there is a very interesting result here:

**SSSF alone nearly ties CAE as-is**, because it is exceptionally strong at execution mechanics.

But it falls apart as the actual CAE architecture because it has almost none of the domain/governance machinery CAE requires.

---

# 12. Is CAE over-engineered?

This is the subtle part.

## Some of it is.

I think we have occasionally over-engineered **the machinery used to execute the architecture**.

For example, if a deterministic operation can simply be:

```python
validate_source_package(...)
```

we shouldn't create:

```text
Agent
→ Skill
→ Subagent
→ MCP
```

just to run it.

## But CAE itself is not over-engineered

Because the problem is genuinely more complex.

You're building a system that has to answer:

```text
What is this thing?
Who owns the meaning?
What state is it in?
What evidence supports it?
What may change it?
Which Program may act on it?
Which agent may reason about it?
Which context is permitted?
Which rule applies?
What is canonical?
What transition is lawful?
What artifact proves it?
What happened afterward?
```

That's not unnecessary abstraction.

That's the domain.

# 13. So I would change the CAE mental model

```text
                    ┌──────────────────────┐

       └──────┬───────┘                 └──────┬───────┘

                           ↓
                    ┌───────────────┐
                    │   HARNESS     │
                    │ hooks/gates   │
                    │ validators    │
                    └───────┬───────┘
                            ↓
                    ┌───────────────┐
                    │   ARTIFACT    │
                    │ + RECEIPT     │
                    └───────┬───────┘
                            ↓
                    ┌───────────────┐
                    │ STATE UPDATE  │
                    └───────────────┘
```

That is the software factory.

`CAE.md` becomes the **filesystem-level context boundary**.

```text
Domain
   +
Program
   +
State
   +
Local
```

with precedence:

That last bit is crucial.

# 17. The killer feature would be runtime context compilation

```text
model
prompt
tools
```

and separately its harness capabilities. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory/tree/example))

```text
+ Context Policy

+ Prompt
+ Tools
```

So SSSF gives us the **operational core**; CAE adds the **governance core**.

# 20. My recommendation

I would **absolutely stick with CAE**.

>

>
> **Code performs deterministic operations.**
>
> **Harnesses enforce execution guarantees.**
>
> **Hooks enforce event-level guarantees.**
>
> **Skills provide reusable capabilities.**
>

>

That is not over-engineering.

That is actually **simplifying the architecture by assigning each concern one owner**.

That becomes unmaintainable.

```text
phase

gate

next phase
```

CAE should preserve that simplicity while adding the semantic/governance layers.

My answer is **not**:

My answer is:

And your `CAE.md` idea is the missing **context-localization layer** that makes that factory practical.

```text
Civil Code

      ↓
Software Factory / executable Program graph
      ↓
Agent + Code phases
      ↓
Harness + Hooks + Validators
      ↓
Artifact + Receipt
      ↓
State transition
```

That gives us **the governance depth of CAE with the execution discipline of SSSF**, rather than forcing either architecture to do the other's job.

And the current CAE repo already has enough Pipeline/Program infrastructure that I would **extend this architecture rather than restart it**. ([GitHub](https://github.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/tree/main/services/pipeline))

Yes. I traced the actual current `services/pipeline` path, and the result is much more concrete-and more revealing-than my previous answer.

The central finding is:

> **CAE has a strong deterministic workflow/context/contract substrate, but the current Pipeline code does not yet show an SSSF-equivalent “agent config → compiled system prompt → agent call → typed envelope → gate” execution path.**
>
> In particular, **the current JIT/context machinery stops at producing a capsule**. I do not find evidence in the current `services/pipeline` code that this capsule is compiled into the `system_prompt` of `ModelReasoningEngine.infer()`.

That is the important architectural gap.

# 2. Where is phase sequencing implemented?

## Answer: `DeterministicScheduler`

Concrete path:

`services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/scheduler.py`

The class is literally named:

```python
class DeterministicScheduler:
```

Its `ready_nodes()` constructs predecessor sets from workflow edges and only returns nodes whose predecessors are `SUCCEEDED`. It then orders them by:

```python
(item["phase_order"], item["node_id"])
```

`safe_parallel_batch()` additionally prevents conflicting non-read-only side-effect classes from occupying the same batch. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/scheduler.py))

So CAE does **not** leave phase ordering to an LLM.

That part is real and deterministic.

Then `WorkflowRunService.dispatch_node()` calls:

```python
self.scheduler.ready_nodes(workflow, states)
```

and rejects the node when it is not ready. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/run_service.py))

### Conclusion

**Phase sequencing: implemented and deterministic.**

This is one of the strongest overlaps with SSSF.

---

# 3. Where is the phase graph itself constructed?

## Answer: `RuntimeWorkflowCompiler`

Concrete path:

`services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/compiler.py`

`RuntimeWorkflowCompiler.compile()`:

1. rejects a non-execution-eligible binding;
2. verifies binding/projection identity;
3. attaches implementation identity/version/hash to every workflow node;
4. carries through workflow edges;
5. carries through `topological_order`;
6. carries through semantic dependencies;
7. carries through wrong-reading locks;
8. carries through evaluation requirements;
9. carries through repair laws;
10. validates the complete runtime workflow;
11. stores it as `runtime_workflow_definition`;
12. creates dependency edges in the repository. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/compiler.py))

The runtime node schema itself requires:

```text
node_id
capability_id
phase_order
purpose
actor_kind
role
product_boundary
input_contracts
output_contracts
side_effect_class
implementation
```

and the implementation binding must include:

```text
implementation_id
implementation_version
implementation_sha256
owner_product
implementation_kind
side_effect_class
authority_boundary
```

The validator rejects mismatched side-effect classes and enforces product-boundary constraints for human gates and external-product nodes. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/domain/models.py))

### Conclusion

The graph compiler is quite serious.

This is not generic orchestration.

# 5. There is a subtle but important thing CAE DOES have: Programmed Model configuration

`ProgrammedModelRegistry` is not an Agent registry.

Its `register_program()` contract contains:

```text
model_program_id
version
claim_ref
input_contract_id
output_contract_id
skill_refs
steering_recipe_refs
allowed_tool_ids
forbidden_action_ids
fallback_mode
escalation_conditions
runtime_requirements
lifecycle_state
```

That is real. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/programmed_model_engine.py))

And `resolve()` chooses a model program according to runtime context:

```text
claim_type
category_id
format_profile_id
role_id
task_type
available_runtime_ids
maximum_parameter_count
required_tool_ids
allowed_lifecycle_states
```

It checks applicability envelopes, lifecycle state, model size, runtime intersection, tools, benchmark threshold, etc. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/programmed_model_engine.py))

So CAE already has:

> **model selection by governed applicability.**

But that is **not the same thing as agent configuration**.

It chooses the model/program.

It does not define the complete reasoning agent:

```text
identity
system instructions
context recipe
tool surface
output parser
harness
```

Then it literally builds:

That means:

I found no Pipeline-level prompt compiler in this path.

That is much more significant than I previously admitted.

# 8. This is where `JITContextCompiler` becomes fascinating

CAE absolutely **does have context compilation**.

`services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/jit_context.py`

defines:

```python
class JITContextCompiler:
```

It compiles:

```text
node_id
implementation_ref
actor_kind
role
product_boundary
context_refs
allowed_actions
forbidden_actions
tool_ids
input_contracts
output_contracts
evaluation_requirements
expires_after_ms
```

and explicitly sets:

```python
"secrets_included": False,
"unrestricted_context_included": False,
```

then hashes the result into:

```text
jit-capsule
```

with a semantic identity. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/jit_context.py))

This is very good architecture.

But notice what `JITContextCompiler` returns:

```text
capsule
```

not:

```text
system_prompt
```

and not:

```text
AgentExecutionRequest
```

and not:

```text
ModelInvocation
```

So the pipeline currently has the **context-control substrate**, but the final **agent-context binding seam** is not established by this code.

# 9. And `dispatch_node()` proves this

`WorkflowRunService.dispatch_node()` receives:

```text
context_refs
allowed_actions
forbidden_actions
tool_ids
```

and passes those into:

```python
capsule = self.jit.compile(...)
```

Then it stores the capsule inside the `NodeDispatched` event:

```python
{
    "node_id": node_id,
    "dispatch_ordinal": ordinal,
    "jit_capsule": capsule
}
```

and returns the capsule. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/run_service.py))

So:

```text
workflow node
 ↓
JIT context
 ↓
capsule
 ↓
dispatch event
```

is real.

But I do not see:

```text
capsule
 ↓
ModelReasoningEngine.infer(...)
```

in this execution path.

That is the seam we were looking for.

# 10. Where is context handed off?

There are actually **two different context mechanisms** in CAE.

## A. Retrieval context

`AuthorityFirstRetrievalService.compile_capsule()` builds a canonical retrieval capsule.

It accepts:

```text
role_id
category_id
format_profile_id
required_source_kinds
required_tags
required_action_ids
required_projection_ids
include_contradictions
include_failed_alternatives
budget_bytes
allowed_tool_ids
forbidden_action_ids
stopping_law_id
source_package_ref
```

and deterministically selects eligible projections. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/retrieval_engine.py))

It also records:

```text
coverage_proof
authority_first
minimum_complete_context
```

and stores both:

```text
jit_execution_capsule_v2
retrieval_receipt
```

with hashes. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/retrieval_engine.py))

## B. Execution context

`JITContextCompiler` creates the execution capsule containing the node's:

```text
context_refs
allowed_actions
forbidden_actions
tool_ids
contracts
evaluation requirements
```

([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/jit_context.py))

### But neither currently proves final prompt injection.

That's the crucial distinction.

# 11. SSSF has the missing final step

The Super Simple Software Factory explicitly has:

```text
agent config
→ phase call
→ prompt
→ typed output
→ gates
→ next phase
```

Its repo says one YAML config establishes the core four:

```text
context
model
prompt
tools
```

and its `ph.call(...)` takes an output type and gates. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory/tree/example))

It is explicit about the actual handoff:

> context transfers in code, not in conversation.

And its output is parsed against the declared output type before gates are evaluated. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory/tree/example))

CAE currently has the **upstream half** of this design.

# 12. What is typed in CAE?

Quite a lot.

This is another place where the code is substantially stronger than my earlier generic description.

### Runtime nodes

Strict required-field validation is enforced by `validate_runtime_node()`. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/domain/models.py))

### Runtime workflow

`validate_runtime_workflow()` requires a complete schema including:

```text
source_projection_id
binding_manifest_id
category_id
profile_id
purpose
semantic_dependency_refs
nodes
edges
topological_order
runtime_projection_digest
semantic_parity_digest
wrong_reading_locks
evaluation_requirements
repair_laws
```

and validates uniqueness, edge integrity and complete topological coverage. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/domain/models.py))

### Handoffs

`HandoffValidator` requires exactly:

```text
producer_node_id
consumer_node_id
output_ref
contract_id
validation_receipt_refs
authority_refs
lifecycle_state
```

and requires the contract to be bilateral-present in both producer output contracts and consumer input contracts. It also requires lifecycle `ACCEPTED`. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/handoff_validator.py))

### Run completion

`complete_node()` requires:

```python
output_ref
validation_receipt_refs
```

and rejects missing/non-unique validation receipt refs. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/run_service.py))

### Model outputs

`ReasoningInferenceResult` is an actual frozen dataclass:

```text
provider_class
model_id
prompt_text
response_text
parsed_json
prompt_tokens
completion_tokens
total_tokens
latency_micros
credential_redacted
receipt_sha256
```

([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/reasoning/model_reasoning_engine.py))

So CAE has **strong typing/contracts around the execution substrate**.

The weakness is not "there are no contracts."

The weakness is **the model boundary is not yet connected to the same contract system with the same strength**.

# 13. What is deterministic?

A lot.

### Workflow sequencing

`DeterministicScheduler`. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/scheduler.py))

### Workflow compilation

Canonical identity and runtime digests. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/compiler.py))

### Context compilation

`JITContextCompiler` produces semantic identity/hash. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/jit_context.py))

### Retrieval

Eligibility is deterministic before optional dense ranking. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/retrieval_engine.py))

### Model resolution

Candidate selection is deterministic and sorted by a declared rank tuple. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/programmed_model_engine.py))

### Run identity

`create_run()` derives deterministic run identity from workflow hash, binding reference, context refs and batch ref. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/run_service.py))

### State transitions

Illegal transitions raise `PipelineLifecycleError`. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/run_service.py))

### Persistence

Canonical JSON and hashes are used heavily.

So the deterministic substrate is **real and substantial**.

# 14. What happens when a gate fails?

This requires careful wording because CAE does not have the same explicit `gates=[...]` abstraction as SSSF in the current path I traced.

CAE instead has several deterministic failure mechanisms.

## Node not ready

`dispatch_node()` rejects it:

```text
node is not ready
```

([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/run_service.py))

## Invalid node transition

`_transition_node()` rejects illegal state changes:

```text
node transition X -> Y is forbidden
```

([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/run_service.py))

## Failed node

`fail_node()` sets:

```text
NodeState.FAILED
RunState.FAILED
```

and appends a `NodeFailed` event. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/run_service.py))

## Required validation missing

`complete_node()` rejects completion. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/run_service.py))

## Retrieval requirement unsatisfied

`compile_capsule()` raises `PipelineValidationError`. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/retrieval_engine.py))

## Budget unsatisfied

It raises:

```text
RET-BUDGET-UNSATISFIABLE
```

([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/retrieval_engine.py))

### What I do NOT find

I do not see the SSSF pattern:

```text
agent output
 → gate
 → automatic feedback
 → same agent/phase repair
 → retry
```

in this traced Pipeline model path.

CAE has **failure and lifecycle machinery**, but not a clearly implemented **agent repair-loop gate abstraction** equivalent to SSSF.

That is an important missing capability.

# 15. What is persisted?

Very extensively.

The run service persists:

```text
pipeline_workflows
pipeline_runs
pipeline_node_states
pipeline_run_events
pipeline_checkpoints
```

The workflow is persisted as canonical JSON with a hash. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/run_service.py))

Each state transition appends events.

`replay()` verifies:

1. sequence has no gaps;
2. each payload hash matches;
3. returns the entire event stream;
4. returns an event-stream hash;
5. asserts historical events were not rewritten. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/run_service.py))

That is significantly more rigorous than a simple execution log.

# 17. What remains model-controlled?

This is the most important question.

In the current concrete Pipeline path:

## The model controls

When `ModelReasoningEngine.infer()` is called, the remote model controls the generated `response_text`.

It can optionally produce JSON, but the code first receives raw text and then tries to parse JSON. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/reasoning/model_reasoning_engine.py))

More revealingly, its parser does this:

```python
cleaned_content.find("{")
cleaned_content.rfind("}")
```

if direct JSON parsing fails. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/reasoning/model_reasoning_engine.py))

So the model boundary is currently **more permissive than the strong typed handoff machinery elsewhere in Pipeline**.

That is a real architectural asymmetry.

## The model does NOT control

The scheduler.

Workflow topology.

Node readiness.

Node state transitions.

Binding eligibility.

Retrieval eligibility.

Model-program selection.

Canonical identities.

Run persistence.

Event sequencing.

Those are code-controlled. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/scheduler.py))

# 18. This gives us an exact CAE vs SSSF comparison

| Concern | CAE current code | SSSF |
|---|---|---|
| Phase graph | `RuntimeWorkflowCompiler` | ADW Python |
| Phase sequencing | `DeterministicScheduler` | code/context-manager phases |
| Node state | `WorkflowRunService` | phase/session state |
| Context retrieval | `AuthorityFirstRetrievalService` | agent context/config |
| JIT execution context | `JITContextCompiler` | phase input/context |
| Agent config | **No equivalent found in Pipeline composition** | `sssf.config.yaml` |
| System prompt compilation | **No equivalent found** | agent prompt files loaded from config |
| Model selection | `ProgrammedModelRegistry` | agent config |
| Tool allowlist | yes, in runtime/model program | yes |
| Forbidden actions | yes | partially via tools/writes/gates |
| Typed handoff | `HandoffValidator` | Pydantic envelope |
| Model output parsing | `parsed_json` best-effort | declared output type |
| Gate abstraction | **not explicit in this path** | explicit gates |
| Automatic repair loop | **not shown** | explicit retry/correction flow |
| Deterministic code phase | yes | yes |
| Persistence | strong SQLite event/state model | SQLite trace |
| Replay | **strong** | observability/traces |
| Hash provenance | strong | present but lighter |
| Authority semantics | **much deeper** | minimal |
| Canonical knowledge | **much deeper** | not its problem |

This is the cleanest comparison I can give you from the code.

# 19. The most important discovery: CAE has TWO halves that currently don't fully meet

I would visualize the current implementation this way:

```text
                    CAE TODAY

        GOVERNED / DETERMINISTIC HALF
        ─────────────────────────────

 Harness
    ↓
 Graph
    ↓
 Binding
    ↓
 RuntimeWorkflow
    ↓
 Scheduler
    ↓
 JIT Context
    ↓
 Retrieval Capsule
    ↓
 Handoff Contracts
    ↓
 State / Events / Receipts

⚠ SEAM

MODEL / REASONING HALF
        ──────────────────────

 ProgrammedModelRegistry
    ↓
 ModelReasoningEngine
    ↓
 hard-coded/default system_prompt
    ↓
 caller-provided prompt
    ↓
 provider API
    ↓
 raw response
    ↓
 best-effort JSON parsing
```

The first half is highly governed.

The second half is comparatively primitive.

And the two halves are **not yet visibly unified by one runtime invocation contract**.

That is the exact finding I was previously hand-waving around.

# 20. This also explains why `CAE.md` suddenly matters

Now your original question becomes much sharper.

The missing thing isn't merely:

> "Where should we store instructions?"

We need a **Context → Agent Invocation compiler**.

Something that takes:

```text
workflow node
+
role
+
program
+
state
+
authority
+
local CAE.md inheritance
+
Skills
+
retrieval capsule
+
allowed tools
+
forbidden actions
+
output contract
+
model resolution
```

and deterministically produces:

```text
AgentInvocation
```

containing something like:

```text
agent identity
system prompt
developer/local instructions
task/user prompt
context refs
tool definitions
output contract
model binding
harness binding
authority refs
context hash
prompt hash
```

**That is the missing bridge.**

---

# 21. And now SSSF teaches us something much more specific

SSSF's code does not merely say "use agents."

It has a concrete primitive:

```python
with run.phase(...) as ph:
    result = ph.call(
        AgentCall(
            output_type=PlanOutput,
            prompt=prompt,
            gates=[...]
        )
    )
```

The phase has an owner.

The agent is named by role.

The output is typed.

The gate is explicit.

The code remains in charge.

The handoff is materialized.

The execution becomes observable. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory/tree/example))

CAE already has equivalents for some of these:

```text
phase        → runtime node
owner        → actor_kind / role / product_boundary
dependencies → workflow edges
output       → output_contracts + output_ref
context      → JIT/retrieval capsules
gate-ish     → validators / lifecycle checks
trace        → event stream
```

But the crucial one is missing:

```text
AgentCall(...)
```

as a **first-class governed boundary joining the runtime node to the model engine**.

---

# 22. I would therefore NOT create "50 more architecture components"

This is where your concern about over-engineering is justified.

I don't think CAE needs:

```text
AgentOrchestrator
PromptManager
PromptEngine
ContextManager
AgentManager
AgentRuntimeManager
AgentStateManager
```

with another 30 classes.

That would be exactly the reward-hacked response you were warning against.

I think there is a much smaller missing seam:

# `AgentInvocationCompiler`

Conceptually:

```text
Runtime Node
   +
Resolved Model Program
   +
JIT Context
   +
Retrieval Capsule
   +
Local CAE.md chain
   +
Skill resolution
   +
Tool/action policy
   +
Output contract
        ↓
AgentInvocation
        ↓
Pi / provider adapter
```

Then the actual model engine receives:

```text
AgentInvocation.system_prompt
AgentInvocation.user_prompt
AgentInvocation.tool_definitions
AgentInvocation.output_schema
AgentInvocation.model_ref
```

That would make the SSSF comparison exact.

---

# 23. And I would make the typed model boundary stricter

Right now:

```python
infer(...)
    → response_text
    → best-effort JSON extraction
```

is weaker than:

```text
HandoffValidator
validate_runtime_node
validate_runtime_workflow
```

This asymmetry bothers me.

For a governed CAE system, I would prefer:

```text
AgentInvocation
  output_contract_id
        ↓
provider
        ↓
raw model output
        ↓
strict contract validator
        ↓
typed AgentResult
        ↓
gate/validator
        ↓
handoff
```

rather than allowing arbitrary `{...}` extraction.

The existing `ModelReasoningEngine` is explicitly described as doing genuine remote inference and capturing prompt/response/token/latency metadata, which is good; but its parsing layer is still permissive. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/reasoning/model_reasoning_engine.py))

---

# 24. And there is one more important finding from the Phase 9 demo

The repo itself demonstrates the pieces separately.

`phase9_demo.py` creates:

- a Skill,
- a Steering Recipe,
- a retrieval capsule,
- a Programmed Model Artifact,
- a Model Claim,
- a Model Program,
- a Model Resolution,

and writes those outputs into separate JSON records. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/phase9_demo.py))

Notice what happens there:

```text
skill
recipe
retrieval
model artifact
model claim
model program
model resolution
```

are all **real artifacts**.

But they are not visibly compiled into:

```text
actual agent system prompt
+
actual agent turn
+
actual typed model result
```

That is exactly the seam I would investigate/build next.

---

# 25. So, answering your ten questions directly

### Where is phase sequencing implemented?

**`services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/scheduler.py` → `DeterministicScheduler`**, invoked by `WorkflowRunService.ready_nodes()` / `dispatch_node()`. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/scheduler.py))

### Where is the agent config loaded?

**I do not find a first-class Agent config loader in the current Pipeline composition.** `PipelineApplication` has `ProgrammedModelRegistry` and `SkillRegistry`, but no Agent registry/config compiler. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/application.py))

### Where does the system prompt come from?

**`ModelReasoningEngine.infer()` receives it from its caller; the default is a hard-coded string in `model_reasoning_engine.py`.** ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/reasoning/model_reasoning_engine.py))

### Where is context handed off?

**Execution context:** `WorkflowRunService.dispatch_node()` → `JITContextCompiler.compile()` → JIT capsule. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/run_service.py))

**Knowledge context:** `AuthorityFirstRetrievalService.compile_capsule()` → retrieval capsule + retrieval receipt. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/retrieval_engine.py))

**But actual model-prompt injection is not demonstrated in the traced Pipeline path.**

### What is typed?

Runtime nodes, runtime workflows, handoffs, contracts, run state, refs, retrieval requests, Skill/Recipe objects, Programmed Model objects, and `ReasoningInferenceResult`. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/domain/models.py))

### What is deterministic?

Scheduler, workflow compilation, canonical identities/hashes, retrieval eligibility/ranking, model resolution, run identity, state transitions, persistence and event sequencing. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/scheduler.py))

### What happens when a gate fails?

There isn't one single explicit SSSF-style gate primitive in this path. Instead, CAE has lifecycle/validation failures: dispatch rejection, invalid transitions, failed nodes, missing validation receipts, retrieval unsatisfied, budget failures, etc. `fail_node()` moves the node and run to `FAILED`. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/run_service.py))

### What is persisted?

Workflow definitions, runs, node states, events, checkpoints, retrieval capsules/receipts, Skills/Recipes, model-program objects and other repository objects. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/run_service.py))

### What becomes observable?

State transitions and execution events, including sequence, payload hashes, run replay, checkpoint and event-stream hash. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/run_service.py))

### What remains model-controlled?

The actual semantic/model response produced by the provider. The model gets a caller-supplied system/user prompt and returns raw response text, with permissive JSON parsing afterward. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/reasoning/model_reasoning_engine.py))

---

# 26. My architectural verdict now

I would **not** say "CAE needs to become SSSF."

I would say:

> **CAE has already built most of the factory control plane. It has not yet completed the governed Agent Invocation seam.**

And that is a much more precise diagnosis.

### Already strong

```text
Workflow graph             ✅
Deterministic sequencing   ✅
State machine              ✅
JIT context                ✅
Authority-aware retrieval  ✅
Skill resolution           ✅
Model resolution           ✅
Handoff contracts          ✅
Canonical hashing          ✅
Persistence                ✅
Replay                     ✅
Failure states             ✅
```

### Not proven / incomplete in current code

```text
Agent registry/configuration       ⚠️
Hierarchical CAE.md resolution     ⚠️
Prompt compilation                 ❌ not evidenced
Context → system prompt binding   ❌ not evidenced
Program → Agent binding            ⚠️ partial / indirect
Typed model-output enforcement     ⚠️ weaker than downstream contracts
Explicit agent gates               ⚠️ not equivalent to SSSF
Agent repair loop                  ⚠️ not evidenced
Agent/sub-agent runtime seam       ⚠️ not evidenced here
```

That is the serious answer.

---

# 27. And this changes what I think our next engineering move should be

**I would not start by writing a giant `CAE_SYSTEM_PROMPT.md`.**

That would be premature.

First we should define and prove the missing runtime seam:

```text
Runtime Node
    ↓
Agent/Code actor resolution
    ↓
Context compilation
    ↓
Prompt compilation
    ↓
AgentInvocation
    ↓
Model/PI execution
    ↓
Typed AgentResult
    ↓
Gate/validator
    ↓
Handoff
    ↓
State transition
    ↓
Receipt
```

Then `CAE.md` becomes genuinely useful because the runtime will have somewhere to consume it.

And **this is exactly where your portable `CAE.md` idea and the SSSF factory approach converge**:

```text
CAE.md
   ↓
context source

Skill
   ↓
capability source

Program
   ↓
workflow source

Model Program
   ↓
model source

Harness
   ↓
execution source

AgentInvocationCompiler
   ↓
compiled agent execution

WorkflowRunService
   ↓
factory control

Receipt/Event stream
   ↓
evidence
```

That, to me, is the actual next-level CAE architecture-not another abstraction layer, but **connecting the very substantial machinery you already built to the actual model invocation boundary**.

---

# 3. And I agree with your idea that Agents should be invokable outside Programs

Your "meeting / review / debate / debugging session" example is excellent.

The repository's own Program structure strongly suggests that an Agent has a role identity distinct from the Program itself.

For example:

```text
ResearchCommanderAgent
KnowledgeCandidateHunterAgent
RelationshipCanonicalizationAnalystAgent
OKFBundleComposerAgent
```

are named independently from:

```text
research_canonicalization_program
```

([GitHub](https://github.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/blob/main/programs/research_canonicalization_program/program_manifest.yaml))

That opens a much better model:

```text
Agent
 ├── can participate in Program
 ├── can participate in Session
 ├── can participate in Review
 ├── can participate in Debate
 ├── can participate in Debugging
 └── can be directly invoked
```

The **Program should not own the Agent**.

It should own the **relationship to the Agent**.

That is exactly how the SSSF model works: its config defines *who the agent is*, while the workflow decides *where and how the agent is used*. The SSSF documentation explicitly says:

> Config defines who an agent is. The ADW call site defines how it is used.

# 12. And SSSF's visualizer architecture is something CAE should steal

Not literally Vue/Bun.

The architectural pattern:

```text
execution
   ↓
```
