# The guiding principle for Mandates 49-60

I would freeze this as the doctrine:

```text
PROGRAM
    defines business workflow

AGENT
    defines reusable reasoning worker

SKILL
    defines reusable capability
```

# The 12 Mandates

## M49 - Agent Constitution + Canonical Agent Registry

### Goal

Make **Agent** a first-class CAE object, independently addressable from any Program.

### Why

Today CAE already has agent specifications in `packages/ca_runtime/src/ca_runtime/agent_team.py`.

For example, `AgentMemberSpec` contains:

```text
agent_id
name
authority_lane
allowed_capabilities
skills
subagents
timeout_seconds
retry_policy
is_commander
system_prompt_template
```

and `SubagentSpec` has the analogous structure. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/packages/ca_runtime/src/ca_runtime/agent_team.py))

But these are runtime dataclasses, not yet a clearly established **canonical Agent registry/package contract** analogous to SSSF's explicit roster.

SSSF answers the question:

> "Who is this agent?"

through `sssf.config.yaml`, with one agent, one prompt, one purpose and per-agent model/configuration. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### Deliverable

A canonical `AgentDefinition` / registry containing at minimum:

```text
agent_id
version
purpose
authority_lane
model_policy
system_prompt_ref
context_policy_ref
skill_refs
tool_refs
capability_refs
harness_ref
output_contract_refs
subagent_policy
lifecycle_state
```

### Production impact

**Very high.**

Without this, Agents remain largely embedded in teams/programs.

With it, an Agent becomes reusable infrastructure.

**Estimated production-readiness gain: +8/100 confidence.**

and the execution loop explicitly retries ordinary exceptions. Constitutional violations fail immediately; operator gates pause execution. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/packages/ca_runtime/src/ca_runtime/agent_team.py))

`state_lifecycle.py` documents:

```text
Execute
→ out_hook
→ before_transfer
→ State Commit
   OR Governed Repair
   OR Lossless Resume
```

and its trace taxonomy includes `REPAIRED`. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/packages/ca_runtime/src/ca_runtime/state_lifecycle.py))

So again: don't invent another retry system.

Unify what already exists.

### Deliverable

SSSF-like bounded pattern:

```text
Agent
→ output
→ gate fails
→ structured failure
→ repair context
→ same phase retry
→ gate
→ continue
```

with:

```text
max_attempts
failure_code
repair_instruction
preserved_context
new output hash
```

### Production impact

**Extremely high.**

A factory without bounded repair becomes fragile at scale.

**Gain: +9.**

But SSSF's major operational advantage is that it provides a dedicated read-only **visualizer**, backed by the same trace database, with sessions, trace waterfall and per-phase tool-call detail. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### Deliverable

CAE Factory Floor UI:

```text
Run
 ├─ Context
 ├─ Agent
 ├─ Prompt
 ├─ Model
 ├─ Skills
 ├─ Tools
 ├─ Tool calls
 ├─ Gates
 ├─ Repairs
 ├─ State transitions
 ├─ Artifacts
 └─ Receipts
```

And critically:

> **read-only observational surface over canonical execution truth.**

SSSF explicitly uses this model. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### Production impact

**Extremely high.**

I would not call the factory production-ready until the operator can actually inspect it.

**Gain: +10.**

# M59 - Full Agentic Vertical Slice

### Goal

Prove the whole factory works with **one real Program and one real Agent chain**.

Not unit tests of separate components.

### Example

Use:

```text
Research Canonicalization
```

because the repository already has:

- `CAE.md`
- Program manifest
- Agents
- Skills
- Tools
- Operations
- Hooks
- PostgreSQL connection
- four authority lanes. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/programs/research_canonicalization_program/program_manifest.yaml))

Run:

```text
Operator
→ Program discovery
→ RUN
→ state initialization
→ agent assignment
→ CAE.md resolution
→ context compilation
→ AgentInvocation
→ Pi
→ Skill
→ tool
→ typed result
→ gate
→ repair if necessary
→ artifact
→ receipt
→ state transition
→ observable trace
```

### Production gate

No "mock" stopping point.

It should prove:

```text
real operator command
real agent package
real model/provider
real context
real tool/capability restrictions
real output validation
real state transition
real receipts
real observation
```

### Production impact

**The highest.**

**Gain: +15.**

This is the mandate that converts architecture into evidence.

---

# M60 - Production Factory Certification

### Goal

Establish the finite certification suite before real-world use.

### Why

SSSF itself is deliberately explicit that its simple factory omits some production concerns such as sandboxing, branch-per-run, merge phases, cloud execution and human-in-the-loop approval. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

CAE already has much stronger authority/state machinery, but now we need a final certification layer over the **integrated agent factory**.

### Certification matrix

```text
Agent identity integrity
Prompt hash integrity
Context hash integrity
Skill maturity
Tool authorization
Authority lane
Tenant isolation
Output schema
Gate failure
Repair
Timeout
Cancellation
Operator approval
Replay
Idempotency
Receipt chain
Artifact lineage
Observability
CLI/operator control
Production isolation
```

Then deliberately inject:

```text
bad context
wrong agent
wrong lane
forbidden tool
invalid output
gate failure
timeout
duplicate command
stale operator decision
interrupted session
tampered receipt
```

and prove fail-closed behavior.

### Production impact

**Extremely high.**

**Gain: +12.**

---

# Why these 12, rather than another giant architectural expansion?

Because the repository tells us something important.

CAE already has the pieces:

```text
CompiledAgentPackage
JITContextCapsule
AgentMemberSpec
SubagentSpec
AgentTeamSpec
AgentTeamRuntime
Program manifest
CAE.md
Skills
Hooks
Program state
Causal trace
Operator runtime
```

Those are real. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/packages/ca_runtime/src/ca_runtime/context_capsule.py))

The next danger would be creating **yet another layer on top of those**.

These mandates therefore deliberately emphasize:

> **compile → bind → invoke → validate → repair → observe → certify**

rather than adding more conceptual nouns.

---

This is how I would actually execute them:

```text
M49 Agent Constitution / Registry
          ↓
M50 Agent Package Compiler
          ↓
M51 Hierarchical CAE.md Resolver
          ↓
M52 Agent Invocation Compiler
          ↓

          ↓

          ↓

          ↓
M56 Standalone Agent Sessions
          ↓
M57 Operator Commands
          ↓
M58 Factory Observability
          ↓
M59 Real Vertical Slice
          ↓
M60 Production Certification
```

There are safe parallel tracks:

```text
M49 ── M50 ──┐
             ├── M52 ── M53 ── M54 ── M55
M51 ─────────┘

M56 ── M57
       M58

M59
 ↓
M60
```

# How much do I think these improve our chance of Production?

I would **not** give you a fake probability like "92.7%."

There is no empirical basis for that.

Instead, I would score the **production-readiness contribution** of the next 12:

| Mandate | Production leverage |
|---|---:|
| M49 Agent Registry | 8/10 |
| M50 Agent Package Compiler | 7/10 |
| M51 CAE.md Resolver | 8/10 |
| M52 AgentInvocation | **10/10** |
| M53 Program→Agent Binding | **10/10** |
| M54 Typed Output + Gates | **10/10** |
| M55 Repair Loop | 9/10 |
| M56 Standalone Sessions | 7/10 |
| M57 Commands | 7/10 |
| M58 Observability | **10/10** |
| M59 Vertical Slice | **10/10** |
| M60 Certification | **10/10** |

The weighted message is:

# These 12 materially improve our production probability.

But only because they address the **execution seam**, not because "more architecture" is inherently valuable.

---

# And SSSF changes our bar

I agree with you on this point.

SSSF gives us a useful external benchmark because it demonstrates, in a compact codebase:

```text
config
→ agent
→ phase
→ prompt
→ typed output
→ deterministic gate
→ retry
→ handoff
→ trace
→ operator observation
```

and it provides actual operator commands plus a visualizer backed by its execution trace. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

However, I would **not** call SSSF "proven production software" simply from the public repository. It has a working stamped `example` branch and demonstrable end-to-end traces, which is strong evidence of a functioning factory pattern, but it also has open runtime issues-for example, an open Windows observability failure and an open invalid-JSON execution issue. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory/issues/2?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

So I would phrase the benchmark like this:

> **SSSF is a proven reference implementation of the Software Factory execution pattern, not proof that every implementation detail is production-grade.**

That's exactly the right level of respect for it.

---

# The architectural score after M49-M60

Today, based on the code I've inspected:

```text
CAE constitutional architecture       ~92
CAE domain/semantic architecture      ~94
CAE workflow/state substrate          ~90
CAE agent execution integration       ~55
CAE operator factory surface          ~55
CAE visible observability             ~45
CAE production certification          ~50
```

After M49-M60, the target should be approximately:

```text
CAE constitutional architecture       ~95
CAE domain/semantic architecture      ~95
CAE workflow/state substrate          ~94
CAE agent execution integration       ~90
CAE operator factory surface          ~90
CAE visible observability             ~90
CAE production certification          ~90
```

Not because we have accumulated another 12 modules.

Because we would finally be able to demonstrate:

```text
                    OPERATOR
                       ↓
                  COMMAND
                       ↓
                    PROGRAM
                       ↓
                AGENT ASSIGNMENT
                       ↓
               CONTEXT COMPILATION
                       ↓
                AGENT INVOCATION
                       ↓
            ┌──────────┴──────────┐
            ↓                     ↓
          MODEL                  TOOLS
            ↓                     ↓
        TYPED RESULT          DETERMINISTIC OPS
            └──────────┬──────────┘
                       ↓
                      GATE
                 ↙           ↘
             PASS             FAIL
               ↓               ↓
            HANDOFF          REPAIR
               ↓               ↓
             STATE ←────────────┘
               ↓
          ARTIFACT/RECEIPT
               ↓
          TRACE / VISUALIZER
```

**That is the point where I would become comfortable saying CAE is actually behaving like a Software Factory rather than merely containing Software Factory machinery.**

And importantly, these mandates are **not a replacement for the existing CAE architecture**. They are the convergence layer that makes the existing `CAE.md`/Program/Skill/Hook/Agent/Pi/JIT/state machinery operate as one system.

The current CAE runtime has an actual deterministic scheduler and workflow compiler.

```text
ADW code owns sequencing
```

**Yes.**

**No.**

Yes - **SDLC is the correct term**, and the distinction you just made is actually more important than the acronym correction.

What you're really pointing at is **workflow engineering as executable engineering**, where every meaningful step has a controlled primitive:

```text
function
condition
branch
loop
retry
timeout
parallelism
join
gate
state transition
rollback
human approval
measurement
```

and the Agent is only one kind of worker inside that machinery.

That is a significantly stronger way to think about CAE.

# 1. I think you have identified a missing engineering discipline for CAE

We've spent enormous effort on:

- ontology
- canonical objects
- Programs
- Agents
- Skills
- Harnesses
- Hooks
- state
- authority
- receipts
- context

But the next question is:

> **How do we engineer the actual workflow itself?**

Not merely:

> "Which agents do we have?"

But:

> **What is the exact computational structure through which information, decisions and artifacts move?**

That is what the transcript is getting at.

A workflow should be something we can reason about almost like a program:

```text
INPUT
  ↓
FUNCTION
  ↓
CHECK
  ↓
IF
 ├── PASS → NEXT
 └── FAIL → REPAIR
              ↓
             LOOP
```

That is a much better abstraction for CAE than "agent orchestration."

---

# 2. And there is current research directly supporting this direction

I found several papers that I think are **highly relevant**, not generic "AI agents are cool" papers.

## A. *From Static Templates to Dynamic Runtime Graphs* - 2026

This is probably the **most important research paper for what you're describing**.

The authors explicitly introduce the concept of **Agentic Computation Graphs (ACGs)** and define workflows as executable graphs that interleave:

> LLM calls, retrieval, tool use, code execution, memory updates and verification.

They distinguish:

- reusable workflow templates
- run-specific realized graphs
- execution traces

and distinguish **static workflow structure** from **dynamic runtime structure**. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.22386?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

That is almost exactly the layer we are talking about.

### Why this matters to CAE

It tells us that our "workflow engineering" layer should probably be treated as an explicit engineering object:

```text
Workflow Template
      ↓
Run Graph
      ↓
Execution Trace
```

That maps beautifully onto CAE's existing architecture:

```text
Program / runtime workflow
      ↓
realized execution
      ↓
trace / receipts
```

The paper also recommends evaluating workflows not only on task outcome, but on:

- graph structure
- execution cost
- robustness
- structural variation.

([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.22386?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**I would make this required reading for the next phase.**

---

# 3. B. *Blueprint First, Model Second* - 2025

This paper is even more aligned with your:

> "functions + conditions + measurable deterministic steps"

idea.

Its thesis is:

> **do not let the LLM decide the workflow path.**

Instead:

```text
expert-defined procedure
      ↓
source-code execution blueprint
      ↓
deterministic engine
      ↓
LLM as bounded specialist
```

The paper reports better performance and efficiency on tau-bench versus the strongest baseline, while explicitly decoupling workflow logic from generative reasoning. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.02721?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

That is almost a direct academic formulation of the transcript's:

> "agents plus code"

and

> "code should control the workflow"

principle.

### This has a major implication for CAE

Our:

```text
RuntimeWorkflowCompiler
DeterministicScheduler
state machine
hooks
operations
```

are **the right kind of machinery**.

The question is whether we are **engineering the workflows themselves deeply enough**.

---

# 4. C. *AutoFlow* - automated workflow generation

`AutoFlow` studies automatically generating workflows for LLM agents, including workflow optimization and evaluation. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.12821?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

It treats workflow as something that can itself be optimized, rather than merely treating the agent prompt as the optimization target.

That is an important conceptual shift:

```text
traditional:
optimize prompt

more advanced:
optimize agent

more advanced:
optimize workflow
```

And eventually:

```text
optimize factory
```

That is very close to where CAE is going.

---

# 5. D. QualityFlow - verification can control the workflow

`QualityFlow` is especially relevant because it makes the **quality checker itself a workflow controller**.

The system can:

```text
generate
→ test
→ quality-check
→ submit
```

or dynamically:

```text
generate
→ quality-check
→ revise
→ revert
→ retry
```

The quality checker can dynamically control whether the workflow continues or changes direction. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.17167?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

This is directly relevant to our:

```text
gate
condition
repair
loop
```

problem.

---

# 6. E. *AgentR* - 2026

This is a newer stateful workflow architecture paper.

It focuses on:

- persistent state
- state transitions
- retries
- asynchronous execution
- recovery
- cost logging
- observability

and reports a deployed prototype rather than merely a conceptual framework. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15264?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

That overlaps heavily with CAE.

But note the distinction:

### AgentR emphasizes

```text
stateful execution infrastructure
```

### CAE emphasizes

```text
state + authority + semantic provenance + canonicality
```

So AgentR is useful as a **runtime engineering reference**, not a replacement.

---

# 7. F. SWE-agent

SWE-agent is important for a different reason.

Its research shows that the interface between the Agent and its environment matters enormously. It introduced a purpose-built **Agent-Computer Interface (ACI)** rather than simply giving an LLM generic tools. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15793?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

This supports something the transcript also emphasizes:

> the workflow is not just prompts.

The **environmental interface itself is part of the engineering**.

For CAE:

```text
Agent
+
Tool surface
+
operation semantics
+
feedback format
+
state visibility
```

are all workflow primitives.

---

# 8. G. LivePlan - monitoring an agent workflow

This 2026 work is especially interesting for your observability concern.

LivePlan separates:

```text
executor
+
monitor/advisor
```

and uses runtime diagnosis to detect behavioral drift and intervene during execution. It reports consistent gains on SWE-bench with relatively low added cost. ([DeepPaper](https://arxiv.deeppaper.ai/papers/2608.06701v1?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

That is extremely relevant to:

```text
workflow
→ observe
→ detect deviation
→ correct
```

rather than merely:

```text
agent
→ hope
```

# 9. There is another useful paper for your exact "code > prose" point

*Plan with Code* explicitly argues that planning in code can be more reliable for orchestration because code:

- represents deterministic logic explicitly;
- supports complex sequences;
- is parseable;
- allows checking invalid functions/syntax before execution. ([arXiv](https://www.arxiv.org/pdf/2408.08335?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

That is almost exactly what you are asking for.

The idea is:

```text
prose plan
```

versus:

```text
executable plan
```

and the latter gives us something much closer to **engineering**.

# 24. One caution: don't over-romanticize determinism

We should be careful here.

The *workflow* can be deterministic while the *agent step* remains probabilistic.

For example:

```text
IF QA_SCORE < 0.85
   → repair
ELSE
   → continue
```

is deterministic.

But:

```text
Agent → write QA explanation
```

is not.

The engineering goal is therefore not:

> "make the AI deterministic."

It is:

> **Make the control system deterministic enough that nondeterministic reasoning occurs inside bounded, measurable, reversible envelopes.**

That is a much stronger principle.

# PHASE V - AGENT EXECUTION FOUNDATION

## M49 - Canonical Agent Object Constitution and Registry

### Reference code first

CAE already has an agent-shaped runtime object:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class CompiledAgentPackage:
    agent_id: str
    lane: AuthorityLane
    version: str
    package_root: str
    cae_governance_ref: str
    agents_guidance_ref: Optional[str]
    instructions_ref: str
    skills: Tuple[SkillPackageRef, ...]
    subagents: Tuple[str, ...]
    capabilities: Tuple[CapabilityProjection, ...]
    tools: Tuple[str, ...]
    connections: Tuple[str, ...]
    hooks: Tuple[str, ...]
    extensions: Tuple[str, ...]
    evals: Tuple[str, ...]
    package_sha256: str
```

`packages/ca_runtime/src/ca_runtime/context_capsule.py` already defines this as an immutable compiled manifest. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/packages/ca_runtime/src/ca_runtime/context_capsule.py))

SSSF independently makes the agent roster explicit in `sssf.config.yaml`, where each agent has its own model, purpose, prompts, tools, harness, and write boundaries. Its stated split is: **config defines who an agent is; the workflow call site defines how it is used.** ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### Mandate

**Establish Agent as a first-class canonical CAE object, independent of any Program.**

Define and ratify the Agent object constitution covering:

```text
identity
purpose
authority lane
model policy
prompt references
CAE.md context root
Skills
tools
capabilities
harness
subagent policy
output contracts
retry policy
lifecycle
observability profile
```

Create a canonical registry and resolution contract.

### Why this mandate exists

Today CAE has enough runtime fields to describe agents, but those definitions are primarily embedded in runtime/package structures. The architectural question we need to settle is:

> **Can `ResearchCommanderAgent` exist as a reusable governed object even when no Research Program is running?**

That is required for your future:

```text
agent
→ Program

agent
→ review session

agent
→ debugging session

agent
→ debate session
```

### Production gate

An Agent must be independently:

```text
discoverable
inspectable
versioned
hashable
resolvable
invocable-by-reference
```

without loading a Program.

### Dependencies

Existing `AgentMemberSpec`, `CompiledAgentPackage`, Program manifests.

# M50 - Canonical Agent Package Compilation

### Reference code first

CAE already scans the agent package directory:

```python
cae_md = package_root / "CAE.md"
instructions_md = package_root / "instructions.md"
agents_md = package_root / "AGENTS.md"

if not cae_md.exists():
    raise ContextCapsuleError(...)
```

It then scans `skills/`, rejects nested `skills`/`subagents`, applies Skill maturity gates, hashes Skill content, and compiles the package. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/packages/ca_runtime/src/ca_runtime/context_capsule.py))

SSSF uses the same very useful philosophy operationally: the factory is stamped into a repo with a predictable configuration, prompt files, harness files, and workflows; the package itself becomes reusable infrastructure. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### Mandate

**Make Agent Package compilation the canonical source of executable Agent identity.**

The compiler must deterministically resolve:

```text
CAE.md
instructions.md
AGENTS.md compatibility layer
Skills
subagents
tools
connections
hooks
extensions
evaluations
capabilities
```

and produce one immutable:

```text
CompiledAgentPackage
```

with:

```text
package_sha256
source refs
component hashes
version
lifecycle state
```

### Why

We should not have several competing ways to construct an Agent.

SSSF demonstrates the value of a very obvious package boundary; CAE already has the beginning of exactly that mechanism.

### Production gate

Same Agent package + same repository state + same manifest inputs must produce the same package identity.

A package cannot become executable if a required constituent changed without recompilation.

### Dependencies

M49.

---

# M51 - Hierarchical Portable `CAE.md` Resolution

### Reference code first

This is already explicit in CAE:

```python
class ContextPrecedenceLayer(IntEnum):
    CAE_CONSTITUTION = 1
    OPERATOR_AUTHORIZATION = 2
    PROGRAM_HARNESS_POLICY = 3
    LOCAL_GOVERNANCE = 4
    AGENT_INSTRUCTIONS = 5
    SKILL_PROCEDURE = 6
```

And the source documentation explicitly states:

```text
CAE Constitutions
> Operator Authorization
> Program/Harness Policy
> Local CAE.md/AGENTS.md
> Agent Instructions
> Skill Content
```

It also records exclusion reasons such as:

```text
BUDGET_EXCEEDED
LANE_MISMATCH
INAPPLICABLE_PHASE
FORBIDDEN_BY_POLICY
OVERRIDDEN_BY_PRECEDENCE
UNCERTIFIED_SKILL
WORKSPACE_MISMATCH
```

([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/packages/ca_runtime/src/ca_runtime/context_capsule.py))

### Mandate

**Turn portable `CAE.md` from package-local loading into a deterministic hierarchical context-resolution system.**

Resolution should support:

```text
/CAE.md
/domain/CAE.md
/program/CAE.md
/agent/CAE.md
/local/CAE.md
```

with inheritance, precedence, exclusion, and hash provenance.

### Why

This is your original insight, and the current code proves the architecture already anticipates it.

The missing engineering question is:

> **What exact `CAE.md` chain is loaded for this invocation?**

That must become a runtime fact, not a human convention.

### Production gate

For every invocation:

```text
cae_md_chain
included_rules
excluded_rules
precedence decisions
hashes
budget
```

must be observable in the compiled capsule.

### Dependencies

M50.

# M52 - Canonical Agent Invocation Contract

### Reference code first

CAE already has nearly all the ingredients in `JITContextCapsule`:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class JITContextCapsule:
    capsule_id: str
    schema_version: str
    workspace_id: UUID
    lane: AuthorityLane
    actor_id: str
    program_id: str
    harness_id: str
    agent_id: str
    model_id: str
    assembled_prompt: str
    included_context: Tuple[ContextItem, ...]
    exclusion_trace: Tuple[ContextExclusionRecord, ...]
```

([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/packages/ca_runtime/src/ca_runtime/context_capsule.py))

SSSF's equivalent is explicit at its phase boundary:

```python
with run.phase(
    PhaseParams(
        name="plan",
        kind="agent",
        owner="planner"
    )
) as ph:
    plan = ph.call(
        AgentCall(
            output_type=PlanOutput,
            prompt=prompt,
            gates=[...]
        )
    )
```

The call binds phase, Agent, prompt, output type and gates. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### Mandate

**Create the canonical `AgentInvocation` object that joins CAE's existing context/runtime machinery to actual model execution.**

It must bind:

```text
Agent
Program or Session
State
CompiledAgentPackage
JITContextCapsule
Model resolution
Tools
Capabilities
Skills
Harness
Output contract
Gates
```

and produce the exact invocation presented to the runtime.

### Why

This is the single most important seam.

CAE already has:

```text
Agent
Context
Model
Program
Harness
Skills
```

but they need one canonical executable object.

### Production gate

A Program and a standalone Agent Session must be able to invoke the **same AgentInvocation contract**.

# PHASE VI - AGENT / PROGRAM EXECUTION CONVERGENCE

## M53 - Program → Agent → Phase Binding Compiler

### Reference code first

Research Canonicalization already declares:

```yaml
state_machine: "RESEARCH_CANONICALIZATION_STATE_MACHINE_V1"

agents:
  - "ResearchCommanderAgent"
  - "KnowledgeCandidateHunterAgent"
  - "RelationshipCanonicalizationAnalystAgent"
  - "OKFBundleComposerAgent"

  - ...

  - ...

  - ...
receipts:
  - ...
```

([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/programs/research_canonicalization_program/program_manifest.yaml))

### Mandate

**Compile Program declarations into executable Agent/phase assignments.**

For every Agent-owned node, resolve:

```text
Program
State
Phase
Agent
Lane
Skills
Tools
Inputs
Outputs
Gates
Retry
Recovery
```

### Why

This answers your original question:

> "Are the orchestrations actually attached to our Programs?"

After M53 the answer becomes demonstrable.

The Program manifest won't merely *mention* `KnowledgeCandidateHunterAgent`.

The runtime will be able to prove:

```text
node_03
→ KnowledgeCandidateHunterAgent
→ HUNTER
→ skill X
→ capability Y
→ output contract Z
```

Every Agent node in a production Program must have a resolvable AgentInvocation before dispatch.

No silent fallback Agent.

# M54 - Strict Typed Agent Result and Gate Engine

### Reference code first

SSSF requires explicit output types:

```python
class EnvelopeBase(BaseModel):
    status: Literal["success", "fail"]
    summary: str = ""
    artifacts: list[str] = []
    notes_for_next_agent: str = ""

class BuildOutput(EnvelopeBase):
    changed_files: list[str] = []
    commit_message: str = ""
```

and gates such as:

```python
gates=[gates.artifacts_exist, gates.files_non_empty]
```

([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

CAE's downstream handoff infrastructure is already much stricter than the current model boundary: its runtime nodes and workflow schemas require explicit contracts, while `HandoffValidator` requires producer/consumer contract alignment and validation receipts.

### Mandate

**Make Agent output contract validation as strict as the rest of CAE.**

Replace "best effort" parsing with:

```text
raw model output
→ declared output schema
→ TypedAgentResult
→ gate evaluation
→ accepted/rejected
```

### Why

The Agent is currently the weakest typing boundary.

A model saying:

```json
{"foo":"bar"}
```

should not be enough merely because it parses as JSON.

The runtime must know:

```text
what output type was required
what was received
what failed
which gates passed
which failed
```

### Production gate

An Agent phase cannot succeed unless:

```text
schema valid
required outputs present
artifact claims validated
semantic gates passed
authority constraints passed
```

---

# M55 - Bounded Repair and Same-Session Retry

### Reference code first

CAE already has explicit retry semantics:

```python
if attempt <= retry_policy.max_retries:
    delay = retry_policy.initial_delay_seconds * (
        retry_policy.backoff_factor ** (attempt - 1)
    )
    ...
```

while constitutional/security violations immediately escape without retry. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/packages/ca_runtime/src/ca_runtime/agent_team.py))

SSSF's better idea is that validation failure does **not** cold-start the whole job. It re-prompts the same live session with the correction. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### Mandate

**Unify CAE's retry/recovery machinery into an explicit workflow repair primitive.**

A failed Agent phase must be able to produce:

```text
failure_code
gate_reports
repair_instruction
preserved_context
attempt_number
```

then continue the same session.

### Why

A retry is not just:

```text
try again
```

It is:

```text
same work
+
new evidence
+
specific correction
```

That preserves context and makes repair measurable.

### Production gate

Each repair must record:

```text
attempt 1
failure
repair reason
attempt 2
result
```

and terminate after an explicit bound.

---

# M56 - Standalone Agent Session Runtime

### Reference code first

CAE already has delegation/session information embedded directly in `DelegationTask` and produces a `StructuredDelegationResult` with:

```text
task_id
session_id
actor_id
authority_lane
status
output_payload
error_details
attempt_count
execution_duration_ms
receipt_id
provenance_chain
```

([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/packages/ca_runtime/src/ca_runtime/agent_team.py))

### Mandate

**Promote Agent Session to a first-class execution mode independent of Programs.**

Support:

```text
review
debug
debate
planning
architecture session
incident investigation
research discussion
```

using the same:

```text
AgentInvocation
Context
Skills
Tools
Harness
Gates
Receipts
```

as Program execution.

### Why

This validates your insight that:

> **Program is an orchestration context, not the permanent owner of an Agent.**

It also creates a clean bridge to future operator workflows:

```text
/agent run ...
/review ...
/debug ...
/debate ...
```

### Production gate

A standalone Agent Session must produce the same class of:

```text
context evidence
invocation evidence
output evidence
receipt
trace
```

as a Program-owned Agent execution.

# PHASE VII - WORKFLOW ENGINEERING + SDLC

This is where I would make the biggest conceptual upgrade.

## M57 - Workflow Primitive Constitution

### Reference code first

SSSF's actual workflows contain explicit control flow:

```python
with run.phase(...):
    ...

with run.phase(...):
    ...

if something_failed:
    ...

retry(...)
```

and its README explicitly says:

> code owns sequencing, retries, and acceptance. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

A second useful reference is `pi-taskflow`, which exposes workflow primitives such as:

```text
dependsOn
join
when
retry
output
model
thinking
tools
timeoutMs
cwd
context
concurrency
```

([GitHub](https://github.com/gscode1/pi-taskflow?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### Mandate

**Define CAE's canonical workflow primitive vocabulary and constitution.**

At minimum:

```text
SEQUENCE
CONDITION
SWITCH
LOOP
RETRY
PARALLEL
JOIN
TIMEOUT
WAIT
HUMAN_GATE
FAIL
REPAIR
CANCEL
RESUME
```

and work-unit types:

```text
AGENT_CALL
CODE_FUNCTION
TOOL_CALL
OPERATION
RETRIEVAL
HUMAN_ACTION
```

### Why

We should stop treating these as incidental implementation details.

They are the grammar of the factory.

### Production gate

Every primitive gets:

```text
schema
semantics
failure behavior
termination rules
observability event
test cases
```

---

# M58 - Executable Workflow IR

### Reference code first

CAE already compiles a runtime workflow:

```python
runtime_projection = {
    "source_projection_id": projection["projection_id"],
    ...
}
```

and each workflow node receives deterministic implementation identity:

```python
"implementation": {
    "implementation_id": ...,
    "implementation_version": ...,
    "implementation_sha256": ...,
    "owner_product": ...,
    "implementation_kind": ...,
    "side_effect_class": ...,
    "authority_boundary": ...
}
```

([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/compiler.py))

### Mandate

**Promote workflow structure itself to an explicit canonical Intermediate Representation.**

It must represent:

```text
nodes
edges
conditions
loops
retries
parallel branches
joins
gates
human gates
timeouts
failure paths
repair paths
```

### Why

Right now the runtime clearly has a workflow representation.

What we need is a stable canonical representation we can:

```text
inspect
diff
validate
compile
render
benchmark
version
```

without depending on implementation internals.

### Production gate

A workflow IR must compile deterministically into the existing `RuntimeWorkflowDefinition`.

No second workflow engine.

---

# M59 - Workflow Control-Flow Compiler

### Reference code first

CAE's current scheduler is already deterministic:

```python
if all(
    states.get(parent) == NodeState.SUCCEEDED.value
    for parent in predecessors[node_id]
):
    ready.append(node)

return [
    item["node_id"]
    for item in sorted(
        ready,
        key=lambda item: (item["phase_order"], item["node_id"])
    )
]
```

It also constrains parallel execution according to `side_effect_class`. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/services/pipeline/src/cmf_pipeline/workflow/application/scheduler.py))

### Mandate

**Make the compiler explicitly realize all approved workflow-control primitives into executable runtime semantics.**

This includes:

```text
condition evaluation
switch routing
loop termination
retry counters
parallel fan-out
join semantics
timeouts
failure routing
repair routing
human suspension
resume
```

### Why

This is where the workflow becomes a program rather than a manifest.

The research direction supports this: *Blueprint First, Model Second* explicitly argues that workflow logic should be codified into a deterministic execution blueprint while the LLM performs bounded subtasks rather than deciding the workflow path. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.02721?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### Production gate

The LLM must not be able to silently alter:

```text
graph
condition semantics
iteration bounds
routing
termination
```

at runtime.

---

# M60 - Workflow Step Contracts

### Reference code first

SSSF's phase declarations explicitly identify:

```python
PhaseParams(
    name="plan",
    kind="agent",
    owner="planner",
    description="..."
)
```

and code phases separately:

```python
PhaseParams(
    name="commit",
    kind="code",
    owner="git",
    description="..."
)
```

The key architectural separation is that the commit itself is deterministic code, not something the builder agent is told to perform. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### Mandate

**Require every workflow step to declare a formal Step Contract.**

At minimum:

```text
purpose
owner
kind
inputs
outputs
preconditions
postconditions
side_effects
timeout
retry policy
failure taxonomy
validator
gate
authority
observability
```

### Why

This is the precise answer to your:

> "functions and conditions to make results measurable and deterministic on EACH STEP"

point.

A workflow step becomes independently testable.

### Production gate

A workflow may not enter production unless every step has a complete contract.

# PHASE VIII - SDLC FACTORY + OPERATOR FACTORY

## M61 - CAE Software Development Lifecycle Factory

### Reference code first

SSSF's own starter workflows include:

```text
adw_plan

adw_plan_build
adw_build_test
```

and the full workflow is:

with deterministic code between agent phases. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

before trusting the domain Programs.

# M62 - Workflow Isolation, Parallelism and Sandbox Semantics

### Reference code first

The transcript/reference factory explicitly moves from shared worktrees to isolated sandboxes so multiple Agents can work independently, then converge and merge. SSSF's repository itself notes that sandboxing, branch-per-run and merge are deliberate later extensions rather than part of its minimal core. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

CAE already has concurrency restrictions through `AgentTeamSpec`:

```python
max_concurrency: int = 4
global_timeout_seconds: float = 180.0
```

and validates delegation topology. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/packages/ca_runtime/src/ca_runtime/agent_team.py))

### Mandate

**Define workflow-level isolation semantics for parallel Agent and code execution.**

Support:

```text
workspace isolation
worktree isolation
ephemeral sandbox
persistent sandbox
parallel fan-out
join
cancellation
first-success / race
cleanup
```

### Why

The next step after deterministic sequencing is safe parallelism.

We should not have ten agents modifying the same environment and then attempt to reconstruct causality afterward.

### Production gate

Parallel execution must preserve:

```text
tenant isolation
workspace isolation
artifact provenance
receipt attribution
deterministic join behavior
```

# M63 - Factory Operator Command Surface + Visual Observability

### Reference code first

CAE already has a strong Program operator runtime. Its trace projection contains:

```python
class ExecutionTraceProjection(BaseModel):
    aggregate_id: str

    program_id: str
```

and the command dispatcher already supports `/pause` with explicit actor/version/state checks. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/packages/ca_runtime/src/ca_runtime/program_operator_runtime.py))

SSSF's operator layer goes further: it ships commands like `just sessions`, `just phases`, `just tail`, `just procs`, plus a read-only visualizer over the trace database. The visualizer is a real Vue/Vite/Bun application, not HTML artifacts pretending to be observability. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### Mandate

**Create the CAE Factory Floor: one operator command grammar and one read-only execution visualization.**

Commands should cover at least:

```text
program
agent
session
workflow
skill
harness
run
observe
replay
repair
```

The visualizer should show, at minimum:

```text
workflow graph
current phase
Agent
model
prompt/context references
Skills
tools
tool calls
conditions
branches
loops
retries
gates
repairs
state
artifacts
receipts
cost
latency
failures
```

### Why

This is the operational lesson I think we should steal most aggressively from SSSF.

CAE already has excellent execution evidence.

**We need to make that evidence usable.**

The operator should not have to open source files or query a database manually to understand:

> "What is my factory doing right now?"

### Production gate

One run must be observable live and retrospectively from the same canonical execution record.

# M64 - Factory Benchmark + Production Certification

### Reference code first

SSSF explicitly recommends proving the complete path with a smoke test before composing larger workflows:

```text
config validated
→ session minted
→ Pi ran
→ envelope parsed
→ events landed
```

and its factory measures runs through the SQLite trace. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

The research direction is also moving toward treating the workflow graph itself as an object to evaluate-not only final task outcome. The recent agentic-computation-graph work explicitly proposes evaluating workflow structure, runtime behavior, cost and robustness. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### Mandate

**Certify the CAE factory by repeated execution against deterministic and adversarial workflow tests.**

Measure:

```text
success rate
repair rate
retry rate
termination rate
schema failure rate
gate failure rate
operator intervention
cost
latency
context consumption
parallel utilization
failure distribution
```

Test failure classes:

```text
wrong Agent
wrong CAE.md
wrong Skill
forbidden tool
invalid output
failed gate
repair exhaustion
timeout
cancellation
duplicate command
stale state
workspace mismatch
tampered artifact
tampered receipt
```

Then certify at least two complete production-like paths:

```text
A. CAE Software Development Factory
B. Real CAE domain Program
   e.g. Research Canonicalization
```

### Why

This is the point at which we stop asking:

> "Did we build the architecture?"

and start asking:

> **"Can it perform the same governed workflow correctly 100, 500, 1,000 times?"**

That is the real production bar.

After M49-M64, I would want this to be true **in code**, not merely in our diagrams:

```text
                                  │
```

# Why I believe these 16 improve our Production odds

Because they do **not** primarily add architecture.

They close six concrete gaps:

| Gap | Mandates |
|---|---|
| Agent identity/reuse | M49-M50 |
| Portable context | M51 |
| Actual Agent invocation | **M52-M53** |
| Typed acceptance/repair | **M54-M55** |
| Agent outside Programs | M56 |
| Workflow as executable engineering | **M57-M60** |
| Software Development Lifecycle factory | M61 |
| Parallel/sandbox execution | M62 |
| Operator command + visibility | **M63** |
| Repeatability/certification | **M64** |

The critical ones for production are:

**M52, M53, M54, M55, M59, M61, M63, M64.**

Those are the mandates that turn the current CAE machinery into a **repeatable factory rather than a collection of sophisticated runtime components**.

---

# One important restraint

I would explicitly add this rule to the phase:

> **Do not create a second orchestration engine.**

**Not completely.** After auditing the actual M49-M64 bundle against the actual StateM paper, I would **not approve the bundle unchanged**.

The good news is that the bundle preserves several of StateM's most important principles. But it under-specifies **three principles that are central enough that I would amend the bundle before execution**.

The paper's core claim is not simply "use state machines." It is a specific control architecture:

1. **State is a context-and-contract boundary.**
2. **Entering a state refreshes local instructions and durable progress.**
3. **Leaving a state requires explicit, checked exit conditions.**
4. **Hooks/checks/guards are part of the transition protocol.**
5. **Runtime state is separate from the reusable runbook/control profile.**
6. **Agent and human share the control surface.**
7. **The system learns selectively from failures by turning lessons into versioned practices.**
8. **The control layer should remain lightweight and preserve broad agent autonomy inside phases.** ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.15089))

That gives us a very useful audit lens.

---

# StateM → M49-M64 audit

| StateM principle | Bundle status | Evidence in M49-M64 | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| State is a context boundary | ✅ | M51 hierarchical context; M52 invocation; existing CAE state referenced | **Respected** |
| State is a contract boundary | ✅ | M57-M60 workflow/step contracts + gates | **Respected** |
| State-entry refresh | ⚠️ | M51 compiles context, but no explicit **state-entry refresh protocol** | **Under-specified** |
| State-local instructions | ⚠️ | `CAE.md` + instructions exist, but bundle doesn't require explicit state-local context projection | **Under-specified** |
| Explicit exit conditions | ✅ | M54 gates, M59 control flow, M60 Step Contracts | **Respected** |
| Edge guards / transition checks | ⚠️ | M59 mentions conditions/routing, but does not explicitly define **edge-level guards + pre-transfer checks** as a protocol | **Needs strengthening** |
| Failed check keeps state | ⚠️ | M55 repair/retry + existing CAE lifecycle, but not explicitly framed as "remain in source state until condition passes" | **Needs strengthening** |
| In/out hooks | ⚠️ | Hooks are preserved, but bundle doesn't make **state entry/exit hook semantics** first-class | **Needs strengthening** |
| Durable run state separate from static runbook | ⚠️ | M58/M64 versioned workflow + state/receipts, but separation isn't explicit enough | **Needs strengthening** |
| Agent + human shared control surface | ❌ | M56/M63 give operator controls, but not shared inspection/editability of the same control artifact | **Not fully adopted** |
| Agent can inspect current state / history | ✅ | M56 + M63 command/inspection surface | **Respected** |
| Recovery after interruption | ✅ | M55, M56, M62, M64 | **Respected** |
| Selective versioned procedural memory | ❌ | M64 benchmarks failures, but does not explicitly turn selected lessons into versioned practices | **Missing** |
| Broad agent autonomy within a state | ✅/⚠️ | M52/M56 preserve bounded Agent reasoning | **Mostly respected** |
| Don't decompose one agent into micro-nodes | ⚠️ | M57-M60 could accidentally encourage over-decomposition | **Needs explicit guardrail** |
| Fixed graph vs open-ended task distinction | ❌ | Not explicitly captured | **Missing** |
| Control layer itself is optimizable | ⚠️ | M64 benchmarks workflow, but not explicitly harness/process adaptation | **Partial** |

The paper makes these distinctions unusually explicit. In particular, StateM says that a state combines **phase-local prompt + entry/exit hooks + transfer checks + state-local artifacts**, and that a failed pre-commit check leaves the run in the current state rather than silently progressing. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.15089))

---

# 1. The most important missing principle: state-entry refresh

This is the one I would definitely fix.

The paper says:

> entering a state refreshes the active instructions and durable task information for that phase. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.15089))

And in its implementation:

```text
state entry
→ in_hook
→ load durable context
→ refresh progress
→ initialize state-local files
→ expose current obligations
```

The current bundle has M51:

```text
CAE.md
→ hierarchy
→ precedence
→ context capsule
```

and M52:

```text
Agent
→ compiled context
→ model/tool policy
→ typed output
```

But that does **not yet explicitly require**:

```text
STATE ENTER
   ↓
resolve state-local context
   ↓
refresh obligations
   ↓
compile current-state context
   ↓
AgentInvocation
```

That matters because a long-running agent should not infer its current state from its old conversation history.

StateM explicitly calls that out as a failure mode. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.15089))

### I would change M51/M52 to require

```text
StateEntry
  state_id
  state_version
  active_context_refs
  local_instruction_refs
  outstanding_obligations
  allowed_transitions
  unresolved_checks
  durable_progress_refs
```

then:

```text
StateEntry
   ↓
Context Compilation
   ↓
AgentInvocation
```

That is a very strong CAE improvement.

---

# 2. The second missing piece: explicit transition protocol

The bundle says:

```text
Workflow
→ condition
→ gate
→ repair
```

But StateM is more precise.

A transition is:

```text
request transition
→ verify edge exists
→ before_transfer checks
→ persistence/out_hook
→ edge guards
→ edge hook
→ commit target state
→ append history
→ target in_hook
```

If something fails:

```text
STAY IN SOURCE STATE
```

and let the agent inspect/repair/retry. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.15089))

M59 currently says:

> "condition evaluation, switch routing, loop termination, retry counters, parallel fan-out, join semantics, timeouts, failure routing, repair routing..."

That's good.

But I would strengthen it to explicitly define **transition semantics**, not merely branch semantics.

This is the difference:

```text
IF test_failed
    → repair
```

versus:

```text
transition(source=test, target=repair)
    requires:
      edge_exists
      pre_transfer_checks_pass
      persistence_complete
      guard_pass
```

The latter is StateM's stronger idea.

---

# 3. The third major gap: static workflow vs mutable execution state

This is very important.

StateM explicitly separates:

```text
STATIC RUNBOOK
+
MUTABLE RUNTIME STATE
```

A single runbook can support multiple runs and agents, while each run has its own:

```text
run_id
current_state
state_entry_id
transition history
hook outcomes
check outcomes
timestamps
evidence refs
```

([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.15089))

Our bundle gestures toward this through Programs, Workflow IR, State, Runs and Receipts.

But it doesn't explicitly mandate this separation as a **first-class architectural rule**.

I would add it.

Because the distinction is powerful:

```text
Workflow Definition
= reusable factory design

Workflow Run
= mutable execution instance
```

That is exactly what we need for repeated production runs.

---

# 4. The biggest missing StateM principle: shared control surface

This is the most interesting philosophical difference.

StateM says the **same runbook** is:

```text
agent-visible
+
human-visible
+
machine-operable
+
editable/reviewable
```

The paper calls this one of its core distinctions. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.15089))

Our M63 currently says:

> "Create a canonical command namespace ... and expose the existing execution truth as a visible factory floor."

Excellent.

But that is **observability**, not necessarily **shared control**.

We currently propose:

```text
Operator
  → inspect
  → pause
  → resume
  → approve
  → repair
```

StateM goes farther:

```text
Agent
  ↔
shared control artifact
  ↔
Human
```

where both can inspect the state/control profile, and permitted changes can become part of the versioned control profile. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.15089))

### I would NOT blindly copy this into every CAE Program.

Why?

Because CAE's constitutional model is stricter.

I would instead define:

```text
Canonical Program/Harness definition
        +
Mutable Run Control State
        +
Operator Control Surface
        +
Agent-readable Control Projection
```

The Agent can **inspect and propose** changes.

The Operator/authorized runtime approves/promotes them.

That preserves CAE authority.

---

# 5. The bundle is also missing StateM's "procedural memory" concept

This is extremely relevant to your original "workflow engineering" goal.

StateM doesn't just record failures.

It tries to turn selected failures into:

```text
versioned practices
```

A practice may be:

```text
state-local instruction
check
constraint
activation condition
verification action
recovery path
```

and the important loop is:

```text
execute
→ observe failure
→ attribute cause
→ abstract reusable lesson
→ encode practice
→ validate again
```

([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.15089))

Our M64 currently says:

```text
benchmark
→ measure
→ certify
```

That is good, but incomplete.

It needs:

```text
benchmark
→ failure classification
→ candidate practice
→ review/generalization
→ versioned practice
→ next controlled run
```

Otherwise the factory measures itself but doesn't **learn at the workflow-control layer**.

---

# 6. We should preserve one very important StateM restraint

This is where I think the bundle could accidentally become worse than StateM if we aren't careful.

StateM explicitly says:

> don't decompose the general-purpose agent into a fixed collection of node-local model calls. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.15089))

Its design goal is:

```text
coarse state
+
broad agent autonomy inside state
+
strong transition control
```

rather than:

```text
200 tiny Agent nodes
```

This matters because our M57-M60 workflow primitive push could inadvertently incentivize:

```text
analyze_1
analyze_2
analyze_3
write_1
write_2
check_1
...
```

That would be exactly the wrong interpretation.

### I would therefore add a CAE law:

> **Workflow primitives govern phase boundaries and consequential control points, not every internal reasoning step.**

That is a very good StateM principle for CAE.

---

# 7. This also affects how I think about our SSSF adoption

SSSF and StateM are actually teaching us two slightly different things.

### SSSF

```text
workflow-centric
code owns graph
agents occupy phases
typed handoffs
gates
repair
trace
```

### StateM

```text
state-centric
state is context boundary
state is contract boundary
entry refresh
exit verification
hooks
recoverable transitions
shared control surface
procedural memory
```

CAE should probably combine them:

```text
              CAE FACTORY

Workflow
  ↓
coarse State
  ↓
StateEntry
  ↓
state-local Context
  ↓
AgentInvocation
  ↓
bounded reasoning
  ↓
StateExit checks
  ↓
edge guard
  ↓
PASS → next State
FAIL → remain / repair
```

That is substantially better than either reference alone for our use case.

---

# 8. I would therefore amend the 16-mandate bundle before execution

Not rewrite it.

**Amend it.**

Specifically:

### M51
Add:

> **State Entry Context Refresh Contract**

### M55
Add:

> **State-preserving repair semantics**

A failed check does not mean "call the agent again" generically.

It means:

```text
remain in current state
→ expose failed obligations
→ repair
→ re-check
→ transition
```

### M59
Add:

> **Formal Transition Protocol**

```text
edge existence
→ pre-transfer checks
→ out_hook
→ edge guards
→ commit
→ target in_hook
```

### M60
Add:

> **State boundary vs internal reasoning boundary**

Do not over-decompose the Agent.

### M64
Add:

> **Failure → Versioned Practice → Revalidation**

### M63
Add:

> **Agent-visible + operator-visible control projection**

---

# 9. One important thing I would NOT adopt from StateM literally

StateM is intentionally optimized around a **general-purpose autonomous CLI agent**.

CAE is different.

We have:

```text
Program
Harness
Atomic Harness
Agent
Skill
Operation
Authority
Receipt
State
Canonical object
Product boundary
```

and a stronger constitutional model.

So we should not suddenly create:

```text
Runbook
```

as a competing CAE object merely because StateM calls it that.

The bundle's existing object-authority rule is correct:

> runtime classes are not automatically constitutional objects. ([bundle `00_CONTROL/04_OBJECT_AUTHORITY_MAP.md`])

That restraint should stay.

---

# 10. Final verdict

## Are the StateM principles respected?

### **Yes, at the architectural level.**
### **No, not yet completely at the specification level.**

I would rate the current M49-M64 bundle:

| StateM alignment | Score |
|---|---:|
| State/context boundaries | 90 |
| State/contract boundaries | 88 |
| Transition enforcement | 72 |
| State-entry refresh | 60 |
| Recovery | 88 |
| Hooks/checks | 82 |
| Shared control surface | 55 |
| Persistent run state | 85 |
| Procedural memory / learning | 50 |
| Agent autonomy within phases | 80 |
| Overall | **75/100** |

So I **would not reject the bundle**.

But I also **would not execute it unchanged**.

The amendments above are small relative to the size of the bundle, and they directly incorporate the strongest parts of StateM's architecture.

---

# The most important revised principle

I would put this directly into the CAE execution doctrine:

```text
STATE
  is not merely a label.

STATE
  is a context boundary
  + contract boundary
  + evidence boundary
  + transition boundary.

ENTER STATE
  → refresh relevant context
  → refresh durable obligations
  → execute entry hooks

WORK INSIDE STATE
  → Agent retains bounded reasoning autonomy
  → deterministic code executes deterministic work

LEAVE STATE
  → run checks
  → run hooks
  → evaluate guards
  → commit only if obligations pass

FAIL
  → remain in state
  → expose failure
  → repair
  → retry

SUCCESS
  → record evidence
  → commit transition
  → initialize next state

AFTER RUN
  → classify failures
  → selectively promote reusable practices
  → version
  → revalidate
```

That is the part of StateM I would consider **non-negotiable for the next CAE wave**. The paper is unusually explicit that this is what turns a state machine from a mere orchestration graph into an externally enforceable, recoverable and improvable control layer. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.15089))

So the answer is: **the bundle is directionally correct, but it needs a StateM hardening pass before we hand M49-M64 to Gemini.**


But there is an important nuance: **M57 does not need to wait for the Agent track.** Your current matrix already identifies M57 as parallelizable with M49-M56 documentation, which is exactly the opportunity we should exploit. `CAE_Next_16_Mandate_Bundle_v1.1.0.zip`

## What can genuinely run concurrently

| Parallel wave | Mandates | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Wave 1** | **M49** + **M57** | M49 establishes Agent authority; M57 establishes workflow primitive semantics. They touch different canonical concerns. |
| **Wave 2** | **M50** + continued **M57** | M50 depends on M49; M57 remains independent. |
| **Wave 3** | **M51** + **M58** | M51 depends on M50; M58 depends on M57. Different surfaces. |
| **Wave 4** | **M52** + **M59** | M52 depends on M49-M51; M59 depends on M58. They can proceed concurrently once those prerequisites are closed. |
| **Wave 5** | **M53 + M54** | **This is the strongest intentional parallel pair.** M53 is Program→Agent→Phase binding; M54 is typed result/gate machinery. |
| **Wave 6** | **M55** + final work on **M60** | M55 depends on M54. M60 depends on M59. Different contracts, so they can overlap. |
| **Wave 7** | **M56** + any remaining M60 closure | M56 needs M52 + M55; M60 is workflow-step contracts. |
| **Wave 8** | **M61** | This is the convergence point. It should not start until the Agent and Workflow foundations it consumes are actually closed. |
| **Wave 9** | **M62 + M63** | This is another strong parallel pair: isolation/concurrency/sandbox semantics vs command/observability surface. |
| **Wave 10** | **M64** | Certification must consume the completed M61-M63 system, so this stays last. |

### The biggest time-saving opportunities

**1. Start M57 immediately alongside M49.**

This is the biggest obvious optimization. M57 is foundational workflow vocabulary, but it does not need the Agent implementation track. The existing matrix already says M57 depends only on the M48 baseline. `CAE_Next_16_Mandate_Bundle_v1.1.0.zip`

So I would **not** run:

```text
M49 → M50 → M51 → ... → M57
```

I would run:

```text
Agent track:       M49 → M50 → M51 → M52 → ...
Workflow track:    M57 → M58 → M59 → M60
```

in parallel.

**2. Run M53 and M54 concurrently once M52’s contract is frozen.**

This is already recognized in the bundle: M53 is the Program→Agent binding compiler, while M54 handles typed results and gates. Their outputs are complementary rather than sequentially dependent.

The important constraint is:

> **Do not let M54 invent a competing contract that M53 relies on.**

Both should consume the same M52 `AgentInvocation` authority.

**3. Run M62 and M63 concurrently after M61 is established.**

This is a particularly good pair:

```text
M61 SDLC Factory
       │
       ├──── M62 isolation / parallelism / sandbox
       │
       └──── M63 commands / observability
```

M63 can build its projection layer while M62 is establishing execution-isolation semantics. The operator surface should consume the canonical state/control contracts rather than define them.

The current matrix already allows M62 ↔ M63 concurrency at the appropriate point. `CAE_Next_16_Mandate_Bundle_v1.1.0.zip`

## What I would **not** parallelize

### M50 and M51

Don't.

M51 explicitly builds on the compiled-agent-package contract. M51 needs to know what constitutes the package before resolving its inherited governance/context.

```text

 ↓
M51
```

### M58 and M59

Definitely not.

M59 is the compiler of the executable workflow IR established by M58.

```text
M58
 ↓
M59
```

### M59 and M60

Not safely.

M60 defines step contracts that the control-flow compiler has to consume.

```text
M59
 ↓
M60
```

### M55 and M56

Not safely.

M56's session runtime needs bounded repair/retry semantics from M55.

```text
M55
 ↓
M56
```

### M61 before the Agent/Workflow foundations close

This is important. M61 is the CAE SDLC factory, so it is a **consumer/integrator** of the preceding runtime machinery, not another independent foundation.

Starting it too early risks designing the factory around unstable contracts.

### M64

Never parallelize phase-close certification with the work it certifies.

The bundle already treats phase-close mandates as non-parallelizable, and that is correct. `CAE_Next_16_Mandate_Bundle_v1.1.0.zip`

## The optimized schedule

I'd actually operate the bundle as **two parallel development tracks**:

```text
TRACK A - AGENT EXECUTION
M49
 ↓
M50
 ↓
M51
 ↓
M52
 ↓
 ├── M53 ──┐
 └── M54 ──┤
            ▼
           M55
            ↓
           M56

TRACK B - WORKFLOW ENGINEERING
M57
 ↓
M58
 ↓
M59
 ↓
M60
```

Then converge:

```text
TRACK A + TRACK B
        ↓
       M61
        ↓
   ┌────┴────┐
   ▼         ▼
  M62       M63
   └────┬────┘
        ▼
       M64
```

That is substantially better than treating M49-M64 as one linear queue.

### One additional optimization I'd make to the bundle

I would change the dependency matrix from a mostly textual description into an explicit **DAG with three statuses**:

```text
DESIGN-PARALLEL
IMPLEMENTATION-PARALLEL
MUST-SEQUENCE
```

That would prevent an execution agent from interpreting “parallelizable” too broadly. In particular, **M53/M54 and M62/M63 are implementation-parallel only after their shared prerequisite contracts are frozen**, while M57 can be developed alongside the entire Agent track.

The bundle itself already contains the right instinct-“Safe parallel design/research is allowed where contracts are read-only and no shared runtime authority is mutated”-but I would make that executable rather than leaving it as prose. `CAE_Next_16_Mandate_Bundle_v1.1.0.zip`

**Bottom line:** the fastest safe route is **two parallel tracks (Agent + Workflow), followed by the SDLC integration point, then two parallel factory tracks (Isolation + Observability), then certification.** That should save substantial wall-clock time without weakening the StateM-aligned transition and authority discipline.

But I traced the benchmark implementation.

### The "domain program benchmark" is not executing the actual domain runtime

`FactoryCertificationRunner.run_domain_program_benchmark()` calls:

```python
self.command_engine.execute_command_text(

)
```

and then considers the run successful when that command reports success. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/packages/ca_runtime/src/ca_runtime/factory_certification.py))

But the command engine's `RUN PROGRAM` implementation is itself creating an in-memory run:

```python
run_id = ...
context_hash = sha256(...)
self._live_runs[run_id] = ...
```

and constructing two synthetic replay events:

```text
RUN_STARTED
PHASE_EXECUTED
```

with:

```text
result = "OK"
```

It is not invoking the actual Program workflow, actual AgentInvocation, actual Skills, actual model, actual retrieval, or actual Program execution path. ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/main/packages/ca_runtime/src/ca_runtime/factory_observability.py))

That is a **major false-proof boundary**.

The observability architecture itself is useful.

The problem is that its benchmark currently proves:

> "the observability simulator can represent a successful run"

rather than:

> "the actual research_canonicalization_program executed successfully through CAE's governed runtime."

Those are fundamentally different claims.

### What SSSF actually does with sessions

SSSF has a very explicit session model:

```text
ADW invocation
    ↓
session.ensure(cfg, adw_id)
    ↓
session directory + SQLite session record
    ↓
named phases
    ↓
agent session IDs
    ↓
context_handoff/
    ↓
next phase / next ADW
```

The important part is that `--adw-id` is not just an identifier. Supplying the same `adw_id` causes later workflows to join the same session, reuse the same `context_handoff/`, and resume the existing agent context through `agent_map.json`. Omitting it creates a fresh session. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

SSSF also records the session centrally in SQLite. Its `sessions`, `phases`, `events`, `envelopes`, `gate_results`, `agent_sessions`, and `processes` tables form one observable execution path. Each event is tied to an `adw_id` and `phase_id`, and the live trace is just a cursor over the same SQLite event stream used for history. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory))

The really important design is:

```text
session
  ├── phase: plan
  │    └── planner agent session
  │
  ├── phase: build
  │    └── builder agent session
  │
  ├── phase: test
  │    └── deterministic code
  │
  ├── phase: review
  │    └── reviewer agent session
  │
  └── phase: commit
       └── deterministic code
```

A phase is the unit of orchestration and trace. The model is not the orchestration system. The ADW owns sequencing, retry, acceptance and handoff. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory))

And a failed phase does **not** cold-start the agent. The harness re-prompts the same session with the correction, keeping its existing context. ([GitHub](https://github.com/disler/super-simple-software-factory))

That is an important distinction from what we were doing in CAE.

# What we're borrowing from SSSF

The important SSSF principle for CAE is therefore:

> **A Session is the durable execution container that can host multiple related Workflows while preserving state, context, history, handoffs and observability.**

The historical CAE transcript itself exposes this lineage. It explicitly references the CCP modular PRD structure, CCF, primitive architecture, Matrix of Edging, JIT Skill Compiler, Mood State, CRAL, SearXNG, and other earlier work. `ChatGPT-Video Editing Syntax Research-20260829-1837.md`

So the omission wasn't isolated.

**The library was biased toward documentation that survived into today's CAE naming scheme.**

That is the wrong preservation mechanism for product history.

---

# Why this happens in long-running projects

This is a very common failure mode in a multi-repo / multi-era product.

Imagine the development actually happened like this:

```text
2024
Research
Experiments
Creative systems
Audits
Formats
Primitive ideas
        ↓
2025
CCP
CCF
CMF
Visual systems
Experience systems
        ↓
2026
CAE architecture
Programs
Governance
Runtime
```

But the filesystem eventually becomes:

```text
docs/cae/
packages/ca_runtime/
services/
programs/
tests/
```

The **latest architecture absorbs the vocabulary**, but it does not automatically absorb the historical reasoning.

So a naïve documentation audit sees:

> “These are the current CAE files.”

and accidentally assumes:

> “These are the files that built CAE.”

Those are not equivalent.

---

# This also explains why CCP feels like the “home”

Your description makes much more sense now.

CCP wasn't simply a predecessor repository.

It was the **environment in which many of the conceptual systems matured**.

CAE is therefore not:

```text
CCP → replaced by CAE
```

It is closer to:

```text
CCP
 ├── CCF
 ├── CMF
 ├── primitives
 ├── experience
 ├── reactions
 ├── visual systems
 ├── editorial systems
 ├── research systems
 ├── operator concepts
 └── production experiments
          ↓
       CAE
```

So CCP is a **genealogical parent and intellectual home**, even when CAE replaces the technical implementation.

That is a very different relationship.

---

# And this is why our 144 library must change

I don't think we should simply make:

**144 → 216**

by adding more documents to the existing method.

We need to change the **ontology of the library**.

I would classify every source into one of these:

| Class | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **FOUNDATION** | Product-defining doctrine or constitutional thinking |
| **PRODUCT** | Directly defines something the user/operator creates or experiences |
| **INTELLIGENCE** | Research, primitives, semantic systems, reasoning models |
| **PRODUCTION** | Formats, syntax, composition, visual/audio production systems |
| **ORCHESTRATION** | Programs, agents, workflows, harnesses, sessions |
| **ENGINEERING** | Runtime, schemas, APIs, state, persistence |
| **GOVERNANCE** | Authority, evidence, evaluation, gates |
| **LINEAGE** | CCP/CCF/CMF historical source |
| **TRANSCRIPT** | Decisions and reasoning not captured elsewhere |
| **METHODOLOGY** | BMAD, Grill-Me, SSSF and related external methods |

Then Atomic Harnesses stop being "some missing files."

They become:

**PRODUCTION + ORCHESTRATION + PRODUCT LINEAGE**

which is much closer to their actual importance.

---

# One other thing I want to correct

The previous 144 document list also mixed **documents** and **code files** in a way that blurred the research purpose.

For the BMAD research phase, we should probably have three explicitly separated libraries:

### Library A - Product Heritage

Everything that explains **what CAE became**.

CCP, CCF, CMF, Atomic Harnesses, visual syntax, primitives, research, audits, transcripts, etc.

### Library B - Product Definition

Everything that defines **what CAE currently claims to be**.

Current CAE PRDs, constitutions, Programs, operator docs, specs, etc.

### Library C - Runtime Reality

Everything that proves **what is actually implemented**.

Code, schemas, tests, receipts, implementation maps, runtime traces.

Then BMAD gets all three:

```text
HERITAGE
   +
DEFINITION
   +
REALITY
        ↓
   RECONSTRUCTION
        ↓
   NEW CAE BRIEF
        ↓
   NEW CAE PRD
        ↓
   ARCHITECTURE
        ↓
   EPICS
        ↓
   STORIES
```

That would prevent exactly the failure we just encountered.

---

## So, bluntly: why did they look like different products?

Because **I accidentally treated the latest architectural layer as the product itself.**

The actual product is larger.

Atomic Harnesses are one piece of the missing product history, but the same problem affects the visual syntax, primitive systems, CCF/CMF intelligence, research/audit material, and the creative-production lineage.

The live repo proves that the Atomic Harness system is still physically present as a major top-level branch. ([GitHub](https://github.com/Remjohn/consciousactivation/tree/main/atomic_harnesses_visual_syntax))

So I would **not trust the 144 library as the final research corpus**.

It is useful as a first-pass CAE control-plane index, but it is **not yet the historical/product library you asked for**.

And honestly, I think this discovery is valuable before we touch BMAD, because it tells us exactly what the research phase needs to repair: **we have to reconstruct the product lineage first, not merely inventory the current CAE architecture.**

---
